#856. League One clubs aim for further curbs on spending as budgets continue to spiral

Wage bills in third tier have increased by 15% this season

‘Luxury tax’ and three-year limits on losses considered

League One clubs want to introduce new spending restrictions to reduce losses by limiting investment from owners.

Clubs in the division voted to tighten the rules last summer by reducing spending limits from 60% to 50% of turnover, and removed a staggered approach to owner investment, so that only 50% of equity injections can be spent on squad costs, with the rest assigned to infrastructure projects. Less than six months later many want to go further.

The Guardian has learned that two proposed models are being ­con­sidered: a fixed cap on owner investment or introducing a version of the Premier League’s squad cost rules, with a £1 levy on clubs for every £1 spent above 50% of their revenue. Sporting sanctions would be applied if spending reached 60%, with the money raised from the levy redistri­buted to other clubs in the division.

The move to introduce more spending curbs comes despite a legal challenge to the existing rules from the Professional ­Footballers’ Association, which launched proceedings in August on the grounds that the clubs had failed to abide by the terms of their membership of the ­professional negotiating and consultative committee.

An attempt by League One and League Two to introduce salary caps of £2.5m and £1.5m respectively was withdrawn in 2021 after the PFA took them to an independent arbitration panel.

Discussions over stricter controls have been taking place for some time, but have been given fresh impetus by the publication last month of the State of the Game report. The first piece of work by the ­Independent Football Regulator showed that 94% of clubs in the EFL and National League are loss-making, and that 32 of the 96 would not survive for a month without owner funding.

The changes last summer reduced the percentage of clubs’ income that can be spent on wages, with mana­gers’ salaries included for the first time, but there is a renewed move to reduce losses, which averaged £7.5m per club in League One last season, up from £5.3m the previous season.

One owner said that further regulation was ­necessary because the clubs had shown ­repeatedly that they could not restrain themselves, pointing out that League One wage bills have increased by 15% this season, and that a top-six budget in the division five years ago would now rank in the bottom three.

Reading and Peterborough have long campaigned for tighter spending controls, but face opposition from clubs such as MK Dons and Wycombe, and it is unclear whether any proposal would gain the two-thirds majority required to be introduced.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

A source at another League One club warned that an unintended consequence would be to create a cliff edge in terms of financial resources with the Championship, which loosened its regulations last season by permitting owners an inject up to £33m over three years, an equity allowance that does not count towards the 85% wage spending/revenue limit.

League Two clubs are also involved in the discussions, although it is unclear whether they will choose to align with League One.

The EFL confirmed discussions were ongoing, although formal proposals have yet to be put to the clubs.

#855. Kompany back at Bayern training after collapse

Head coach Vincent Kompany has returned to Bayern Munich's training ground after collapsing at the end of last month.

The 40-year-old former Manchester City captain was taken to hospital after falling ill while watching the club's second team train.

Kompany was diagnosed with meningeal irritation - an inflammation of the protective membrane surrounding the brain and spinal cord.

Bayern said in a statement: "Vincent Kompany is on the road to recovery and has been back at the training ground since the start of the week."

However, the Bundesliga leaders did not hold a training session, with most players away on international duty.

English coach Aaron Danks has been in charge during Kompany's absence, leading Bayern to four victories and a draw.

They face Cologne next on 20 November after the end of the two-week international break.

#854. NASA's twin ESCAPADE Mars probes slingshot around Earth in unprecedented double 'gravity assist'

"No NASA mission has ever done this before."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Twin NASA spacecraft are wrapping up a year-long escapade, ready to make a beeline to the Red Planet.

The Escape and Plasma Acceleration and Dynamics Explorers (ESCAPADE) spacecraft launched in November 2025 on the second-ever flight of Blue Origin's New Glenn rocket. But rather than head straight to Mars, the two spacecraft dawdled through a looping trajectory. Now, they are back in Earth's neighborhood where they tackled a crucial engine burn unusually close to Earth that — if all goes well — will set them on track for Mars.

"No NASA mission has ever done this before," said Rob Lillis, a planetary and space physicist at the University of California, Berkeley and principal investigator of the ESCAPADE mission. "For most missions, it just isn't necessary."

That's because traditionally NASA's Mars missions have been carefully choreographed within cosmic launch constraints, leaving Earth during a brief window of planetary alignment that only occurs every 26 months. ESCAPADE was meant to launch in October 2024, when Earth and Mars were favorably aligned, but delays with the New Glenn rocket forced the mission to sit out the precious launch window.

Rather than wait to launch this fall, NASA decided to try something new. ESCAPADE mission planners designed a "loitering" orbit, shaped like a kidney bean. It called for the twin probes to loop through that trajectory to be back at Earth in early November 2026, ready to continue on to Mars.

Once they arrived, however, the twin probes faced a major hurdle: Each had to perfectly execute an engine burn within Earth's gravity well. The maneuver is similar to the slingshot flybys that spacecraft regularly conduct to adjust their trajectories — but here, the probes had to fire their engines to amp up the effect of the burn rather than acting alone.

The first spacecraft tackled the feat on Nov. 7; the second did so on Monday (Nov. 9). And according to NASA, the burns went perfectly. "This is the first time NASA has used a powered Earth flyby to propel a spacecraft toward Mars, and we've now executed this maneuver twice, flawlessly, in just two days," Asal Naseri, acting associate flight director for NASA's Heliophysics Division said in a statement.

After just a few minor course corrections, ESCAPADE will be sailing toward a September 2027 Mars arrival.

The twin ESCAPADE spacecraft have made the most of their extended tour. Each spacecraft is about the size of two refrigerators and equipped with three scientific instruments and a couple cameras. All are tailored for studying the strange magnetic field of Mars, which is created both globally by charged particles from the sun interacting with the atmosphere and locally by areas of highly magnetic crust.

Earth's magnetic field is much stronger and generated by the planet's core. But it too is affected by the solar wind, as scientists call the constant stream of charged particles flowing off the sun and across space. On the side of Earth opposite the sun, the solar wind stretches the magnetic field to form an elongated tail structure, like a terrestrial windsock.

A range of missions have studied this magnetotail at various points up to nearly 800,000 miles (1.27 million kilometers) away from Earth, but beyond that, it has been a mystery. Conveniently, the two ESCAPADE spacecraft traveled through the structure over the course of about 10 days early last year at a much greater distance from Earth — some 1.19 million miles (1.91 million km) away.

"We were able to capture the magnetic field structure of that distant tail, how it flaps, how it moves, how the plasma flows within it," Lillis said, gathering data that he called "unprecedented." "And not only that but for the first time, we were able to do that with two spacecraft simultaneously."

A second shot at the magnetotail came over the summer, when the spacecraft were much closer to Earth but the moon was also passing through the magnetic structure. The two ESCAPADE spacecraft were able to partner with twin ARTEMIS-THEMIS spacecraft at the moon to observe the structure from four different perspectives simultaneously.

That's a huge boon when trying to study the magnetotail and its intricate and ever-changing magnetic field lines and plasma, Lillis said. "These are generally not things you can measure remotely," he said. "You kind of have to be there."

Meghan Bartels is a freelance science journalist based in New York City who worked on staff for Space.com from 2018 to 2023. Her writing has also appeared in outlets including Scientific American, Science News, Wired, Newsweek and Audubon.

#853. Top four teams in Fifa rankings set to be kept apart until semi-finals at 2027 Women’s World Cup

Team must win World Cup group to trigger rule

Spain, US, Germany and England currently in top four

The top four ranked teams will be separated until the semi-finals at the 2027 Women’s World Cup, ­provided they each win their group, after a change to the tournament’s draw procedure was confirmed by Fifa.

Spain, USA, Germany and England are ranked one to four in the world respectively, although USA and England still need to qualify for the tournament. The seedings will be based on the 7 December updated rankings, meaning the standings could change before the draw, which will take place on 11 December in Rio de Janeiro.

The top four sides were also ­separated until the semi-finals of the 2026 men’s World Cup, which consisted of 48 teams, but it was not announced until Wednesday that the same rule would apply to the 32-team ­women’s tournament. In the men’s World Cup the top four – Spain, Argentina, France, and England – all reached the semi-finals.

The record four-time champions USA face El Salvador on 27 November as they aim to confirm their place at the tournament next summer. A victory, coupled with no changes to the world rankings, would ensure USA would be placed in the opposite half of the draw to the defending cham­pions, Spain. That would mean if they win their groups the two teams could not meet until the final, which will be played at the ­Maracanã Stadium on 25 July. Neither Spain nor USA finished top of their group at the previous World Cup.

England, the 2023 runners-up, must beat Ukraine over two legs on 1 and 5 December to ensure their qualification. The European ­champions hold a 31-point advantage over fifth-placed Japan in the world rankings before the upcoming round of internationals.

France, the hosts Brazil and ­Sweden – who finished third at three of the past four World Cups, and face Scotland in their qualifying playoff in December – would complete the set of eight Pot 1 seeds for the eight groups, if the top eight remains as it is. ­Canada, ranked ninth in the world, could pounce on a Pot 1 spot if anyone slips up.

Fifa has also confirmed that the draw will take place at 1.30pm local time (11.30am EST/4.30pm GMT) on 11 December, at Rio de Janeiro’s Museum of Modern Art. Brazil, as hosts, will be placed in Group A and will contest the opening match at the Maracanã on 24 June.

After the eight Pot 1 sides, the next eight highest-ranked teams involved will be in Pot 2, with the next eight below them in Pot 3. Pot 4 will include three places for the winners of the inter-confederation playoff ­tournament that will conclude in March, along with the lowest-ranked sides involved. No group will be permitted to include more than one team from the same continent, except for European teams, of whom there can be a maximum of two per group.

Fifa also confirmed later on Wednesday that the uncontested bids to host the 2031 and 2035 Women’s World Cups have both passed their extensive bid evaluations.

The US, Mexico, Costa Rica and Jamaica are bidding to jointly host the 2031 event and they received an overall score of 4.4 out of 5. The UK is the sole bidder for 2035 and the bid – which includes a proposal for Wembley to host the final – received a score of 4.3 out of 5.

No venue has yet been specified to stage the 2031 final. Both bids’ infrastructure, stadiums and accommodation were praised by Fifa. Fifa’s congress is expected to formally appoint them as hosts on 23 November.

#852. Wenger considers standing against Infantino

Arsene Wenger (left) joined Fifa as chief of global football development in 2019

Former Arsenal manager Arsene Wenger is considering standing against Gianni Infantino as a candidate in Fifa's presidential election.

For weeks, senior figures in European football have been hoping the Frenchman would run for the job, and he is now giving it serious thought.

Wenger is 77, leading to questions over whether he could provide long-term leadership for the sport.

But some of his supporters have told BBC Sport that they would be happy for him to win the election, then stand down before serving a full four-year term.

Infantino's position was plunged into crisis by a backlash caused by his failed plan to sell commercial stakes in the World Cup to private investors.

But he retains support in South America, Africa and Asia, and recently insisted he has the backing of the "vast, vast majority" of world football.

Infantino laughs off resignation questions

However, that support could be tested if Wenger stands.

Fifa's head of global development would have the backing of Uefa, which has spearheaded opposition to Infantino, and he has credibility throughout the footballing world.

Sources close to Wenger say he is yet to decide whether to stand, and they still believe Infantino is favourite to win a fourth and final term in next year's election.

The deadline for candidates to confirm they are standing against Infantino for the election in March is 18 November.

Former Tottenham defender Ramon Vega was the first person to put his name forward in October.

Japan Football Association honorary president Kozo Tashima has also announced his intention to stand.

This month Fifa said "key documents" relating to Infantino's plan to sell stakes in the World Cup would be made available to members of its council, but they will have to travel to its Zurich base, and access will be under "strict protocols".

Last month Uefa gave football's world governing body until 2 November to release details about the controversial Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal, and to answer questions relating to its decision-making.

That followed a council meeting at which Infantino apologised for the abandoned sell-off plot but failed to explain how the proposal was devised, asking that questions be submitted in writing.

Amid the fallout over FFE, Wenger, who has traditionally been loyal to Infantino, distanced himself from the aborted plot.

"I was not involved in this strategic plan and first became aware of the project through media reports," Wenger said at the time.

"The decision to withdraw the project was absolutely necessary and beyond question, because I firmly believe in an independent Fifa that serves our game with commitment, transparency and integrity."

Wenger has caused controversy at times in his Fifa role, notably for proposals such as biennial World Cups and a "daylight" offside law.

But he also has a global profile, including in Africa, where Infantino recently received a major re-election boost when receiving the backing of all 54 member national associations after promising an increase in funding.

Known as a champion of African players when in charge at Arsenal, Wenger's support of an expanded 48-team World Cup in order to drive development in countries beyond the game's traditional powers has been well received in the continent.

#851. Salty grains in Saturn’s outermost ring formed from the slow freeze of plumes from the moon Enceladus

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Kevin P. Hand is at the Jet Propulsion Laboratory, Pasadena, California 91109, USA.

Saturn is surrounded by eight rings of ice and rock fragments, with the E ring being the outermost one. Supplied with material mainly by the erupting ice plumes of Enceladus, one of Saturn’s moons, the E ring continues to inform studies of planetary science and astrobiology. Now, nine years after the Cassini spacecraft transmitted its last gasp of data from Saturn back to Earth, Postberg et al.1 report in Science Advances the latest analysis of the grains that make up the E ring. They also discuss what these data can tell us about the subsurface ocean of Enceladus, including whether it could be habitable.

#850. US withdraw from U-17 World Cup in Qatar due to safety concerns

USSF cites state department advisory about Qatar

Competition set to kick off in eight days

The US men’s national team have pulled out of the Fifa U-17 World Cup, which is due to kick off in Qatar in just over a week. In a letter sent to players explaining the decision, the US Soccer Federation cited safety concerns for players and staff, referring them to the US state department’s travel advisory for Qatar, which encourages citizens to reconsider travel to the country “due to risk of armed conflict” and asks government employees to obtain special authorization to do so.

“Unfortunately, in light of current circumstances … we are no longer able to participate in the tournament,” US Soccer’s letter to players reads. “The wellbeing of our players and staff will always be our top priority.

“Please accept our deepest appreciation for your commitment to US Soccer and our shared disappointment about these circumstances.”

A US Soccer spokesperson said the federation would not go into details about how it reached its decision. The Guardian understands Fifa was informed of the federation’s decision on Wednesday.

Fifa’s regulations for the U-17 World Cups stipulate that qualified nations must participate in the tournament or be fined, with withdrawal within 30 days of the tournament’s start resulting in a fine of CHF20,000 (about $24,000). Fifa has been approached for comment.

The ongoing situation in the Middle East – involving interconnected conflicts among multiple states – has already led to postponements or cancellations of international sporting events. The 2027 Asian Cup, the continental soccer championship, was due to be held in Saudi Arabia in January 2027 but has been postponed nearly a year due to the conflict between the Saudis and the Houthi rebels, and the Iran war. More recently, Qatar pulled out of hosting rugby’s 2028 Nations Championship finals due to uncertainty around the conflicts. The final races of the Formula One season are still going ahead in the Middle East, on 29 November in Qatar and then 6 December in Abu Dhabi.

Multiple missile strikes by the Houthis on Riyadh’s international airport killed 13 people and wounded hundreds in October. Later that month, US diplomats were told to leave Saudi Arabia amid ongoing Houthi attacks.

Qatar has been acting as a mediator in talks between the US and Iran aimed at ending the countries’ conflict, which started with attacks by the US and Israel on Iran earlier this year. A tanker off the coast of Qatar was attacked in October amid thetensions.

Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.

The U-17 World Cup is still due to begin on 19 November in Doha. The US were placed in Group J along with Montenegro, Algeria and Chile. The US roster that was due to compete in the tournament does not contain any household names, but features a number of promising young players in MLS and abroad.

#849. Birthdays and broken lamps - at home with the Charles brothers

Watch: Cleaning, shirt swaps & video games - the Charles bros at home

Pierce Charles can't help but smile as he waits for Shea to walk into the kitchen.

It's Shea's 23rd birthday and he has a cake to surprise him, something he knows will embarrass his older brother.

Right on cue, he gets the response that he was looking for as Shea has a sheepish smile, and Pierce launches into a rendition of 'Happy Birthday' for the cameras.

In an exclusive interview at their London home, the brothers talk about breaking lamps while playing football as kids, debating who does the chores and the upcoming release of video game Grand Theft Auto VI.

With a cup of tea offered and shoes off at the door, you wouldn't think you were chatting with two international footballers, especially two who are riding the crest of a wave on the pitch.

London traffic aside, they are enjoying life in the hustle and bustle of the city as they live in England's capital for the first time.

"It's better than I thought it was going to be, I didn't think I was going to enjoy it," said Pierce who is spending the season on loan at Queens Park Rangers from Manchester City.

"I actually love it, and living together has been good. There's so much to do in London," added midfielder Shea, who joined Fulham from Southampton in a Â£30m move in August.

Using international football to reignite Premier League dreams

NI win in Georgia after Kvaratskhelia penalty miss

It is the first time the brothers have lived in London, but the third time they have lived together.

Having been born and grown up in Manchester, they came through Manchester City's academy before Pierce joined Sheffield Wednesday aged 16.

Shea stayed at the Etihad and made his Premier League debut under Pep Guardiola in May 2023 before signing for Southampton that summer.

The brothers were reunited at Wednesday when Shea joined on loan for the 2024-25 campaign, but there was some 200 miles between them last year as the midfielder returned to St Mary's.

This summer, after impressive performances for Wednesday and Northern Ireland, Pierce returned to Manchester City in a long-term deal before joining QPR on loan.

Not to be outdone, Shea earned a switch back to the Premier League with Fulham as he became Northern Ireland's first Â£30m footballer.

Both based in west London, that gave them the opportunity to move back in together, reigniting debates over who is better at the Grand Theft Auto games and Fortnite and who cooks the better steak sandwich.

They both want to claim top honours, but Pierce feels he will have the edge if he can get the peppercorn sauce recipe off the chef at QPR.

Older brother Eoin and parents Mary and Kelvin often come to visit, too, and there's more debate over who makes the house presentable, and whether doing the dishwasher actually counts as a chore.

"I think she secretly wants it to be messy, so she can have a little dig at us and do it anyway," jokes Pierce about Mary, who was born in Northern Ireland.

"She enjoys it really, she's not on holiday," Shea laughs.

Quickly realising the danger of getting a telling off on her next visit, Shea adds, "Mum is class. We appreciate mum".

Things quickly get competitive between the brothers over a game of two touch

Before the brothers sit down for a chat, there's time for a kick about in the garden for a game of 'two touch'.

It doesn't take long for their competitive side to shine through, and a best of three quickly becomes best of five then, eventually, a rematch.

Conversation turns to memories of similar games in the family garden as kids and how things used to always take a similarly competitive turn.

"When we used to play Wembley I would have always beaten you two and the loser went in nets," said Shea.

"If you want a fun fact, people might think he is the best player now but Shea was actually the worst out of us when we were younger in the back garden," Pierce was quick to respond.

"It was me, then Eoin and then Shea. To be fair, he's improved massively since."

There's a blame game over a broken clock and lamp, and middle child Shea has to plead his innocence over the latter.

"I broke the clock but I didn't break the lamp. It actually wasn't me, I swear," recalled Shea, still pleading his case before a mischievous "I loved that lamp" almost makes him look guilty.

'No candles?' - Pierce's birthday surprise for Shea

Watch on BBC iPlayer and BBC Two NI from19:15 GMT; Listen on BBC Sounds and BBC Radio Ulster; Watch, listen, live text and clips on BBC Sport app & website

Fourteen years on from watching the Olympics, Pierce Charles made a late double save to earn QPR a draw at West Ham's London Stadium

The brothers have yet to hit London's tourist spots since moving to the capital, but a trip to Thorpe Park just outside the city is on the cards.

Their first memories of London are from visiting their cousins growing up, and there have been trips to Wembley to see childhood club Manchester City.

But the London 2012 Olympics stand out as an early memory, when the brothers would have been eight and nine years of age.

They remember meeting Team GB heptathlete Katarina Johnson-Thompson and recall racing outside of the London Stadium.

"There were little events on outside the stadium," Shea recalled.

"Like the 50 metres and that sort of stuff. I won my race."

Now the home of West Ham United, both brothers have played at the ground this season, some 14 years on from watching the Olympics at the same venue.

When QPR visited West Ham in October, Pierce was the hero as he saved Jarrod Bowen's last-gasp penalty to deny the Hammers three points.

His man of the match trophy from that game is proudly displayed in their home.

"It looks so much different from what I remember," said Shea on the London Stadium.

"And then we're playing in it 14 years later," added Pierce.

"It's mad, we're getting on a bit aren't we?"

Pierce and Shea Charles both had big moments as Northern Ireland won in Georgia in September

The Charles brothers are just two players in a young and exciting Northern Ireland squad.

Michael O'Neill's side currently top Group B2 in the Nations League after four matches, and they have yet to concede a goal.

The campaign started in Georgia in September and both Shea and Pierce played their part in a famous win.

Pierce saved a penalty from Paris Saint-Germain star Khvicha Kvaratskhelia, and also made another big intervention to deny Georges Mikautadze.

Then, nine minutes into additional time, Shea popped up with a late winner to kick-start a window that would see Northern Ireland top their Nations League group after four matches, without conceding a goal.

"I think that's what started the good run," said Pierce.

"You can't win a game like that and fall off."

Highlights: Northern Ireland leave it late to beat Georgia

Now, Northern Ireland will look to finish the job as they host Ukraine in Belfast on Saturday, and finish the campaign in Hungary on 17 November.

"Two wins would be the dream and it would set us up nicely for the next few years," said Pierce.

"The next few games will be tough but we can't wait."

Given they live together and will be in Northern Ireland camp side-by-side - do they get sick of each other?

"It feels like I can't get away from you when we're on camp, but at least it's not shared rooms," said Shea.

"We're just joined at the hip," said Pierce, who added he doesn't get fed up with spending time with his brother.

"We're always together but we're not always together, if you know what I mean."

#848. Thomas Tuchel keeps laser focus on ‘unfinished business’ with England

Head coach did not insert release clause into contract

Tuchel ‘open to everything’ including staying after Euros

Thomas Tuchel will not be going anywhere before Euro 2028. Mauricio Pochettino is expected to leave his role as the USA men’s head coach to replace Michael Carrick at Manchester United, but Tuchel has not lost his passion for international football and has revealed he did not insert a release clause when he extended his deal as England’s manager this year.

It will not matter whether there is an approach from a big club before the next tournament. United can pay about £7m to get Pochettino out of his deal, but the Football Association does not have to worry about being forced to let Tuchel go. “There’s no intention [of leaving],” Tuchel said. “I signed the contract. I want to stay until the Euros. I want to do the Euros. We have unfinished business.”

Tuchel, a Champions League winner with Chelsea in 2021, did not rule out a return to club management one day. He admitted to missing “the 50 matches” a season, “these two minutes when everything is done, before the whistle goes … it’s like the best two minutes”. But while he loves the daily grind, he added there were downsides to playing every four days and there was a twinkle in his eye when he was asked about potentially staying with England beyond the European Championship.

“I am open to everything,” he said, perhaps reflecting that it is not so long ago that people were calling for his head after England’s World Cup semi-final defeat by Argentina.

The mood has improved. Tuchel sounds energised after England’s bright start to their Nations League campaign. His contract contains a performance-related clause that would have allowed the FA to sack him had England underperformed at the World Cup, but Tuchel has support from Mark Bullingham, the chief executive, and Dan Ashworth, the chief football officer.

Ashworth and Bullingham reinforced the message in person during the summer. “They made it very early in the World Cup,” Tuchel said, explaining that the backing came while the sacking clause remained active. “They just made it very clear and it comes from a place of trust, and that’s what you look for as a coach.

“I love my players. I love my staff and I have bosses who trust me. I know how to appreciate it a lot. I miss my players, and I miss my team, and I miss the 50 matches that I’m not involved in a year. But I’m desperate to win the Nations League and to try to win the Euros.”

Tuchel, who is preparing for the Nations League game at home against Croatia on Thursday night, is thinking ahead. He is gearing up for a European Championship staged mainly in England, who would also like to be chosen to host the Nations League finals next summer. “To have it here would be exciting,” Tuchel said. “First of all, we need to reach the final.”

England need one point from their final two games in Group A3 to finish in the top two and qualify for the quarter-finals in March. Victory against Croatia would give them a chance of finishing top when they visit Spain on Sunday. The Croatia game will not merely be a celebration of Harry Kane’s Ballon d’Or. Wembley will watch the captain break the England men’s appearance record, but other issues are at play.

Tuchel needs Jude Bellingham to be careful given that England’s No 10 is on a booking and at risk of missing the Spain game through suspension. There are unknowns in central defence after Marc Guéhi’s withdrawal. Ezri Konsa is unavailable against Croatia and targeting a return against Spain. Tuchel, who added James Hill and Dan Burn to his squad this week, will use a new partnership against Slaven Bilic’s side.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

It is likely to be Jarell Quansah as the right centre-back while Jarrad Branthwaite could miss out to Burn on the left. “Jarrad is doing very well but it’s a very different style of play for him from Everton towards us,” Tuchel said. “Dan Burn is more used to the style with Newcastle from the last two seasons where they followed in a high press.”

Burn led the team out when England trained on Wednesday. Among the group are exciting newcomers who inevitably command the attention. Tuchel has Rio Ngumoha and Josh King in attack. He is the first senior manager to work with the Bellingham brothers. Jobe Bellingham, who has impressed with his physicality and calmness on the ball, plays a deeper midfield role than Jude. Jobe is likely to start on the bench.

Tuchel wants to reconnect with the values from the previous camp. It featured England impressing in a narrow defeat by Spain, before they crushed Croatia 7-0 in Rijeka. One big highlight from the Croatia win was Alex Scott’s performance alongside Elliot Anderson in midfield.

Scott, who is out with a thigh injury, can challenge Declan Rice. The competition for places is fierce. Rice is back after missing the last camp. Tuchel said the Arsenal midfielder remained crucial.

“Declan understands the game like he’s almost a coach on the field,” Tuchel said, but a new identity is forming. It was interesting that Tuchel mentioned the young Chelsea defender Josh Acheampong, whose first call-up may not be far away. It seems Tuchel 2.0 is taking shape.

#847. Total solar eclipse 2027 vs 2028 — Which one should you choose, Egypt or Australia?

From six minutes of darkness in Egypt or totality over the Australian Outback, here are the pros and cons of the next two total solar eclipses.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

For those who want to experience a total solar eclipse, the next two years present the best kind of problem. On Aug. 2, 2027, the so-called "eclipse of the century" will sweep across southern Spain, North Africa and the Middle East, bringing more than six minutes of totality to parts of Egypt. Then, on July 22, 2028, another exceptionally long total solar eclipse will cross Australia, putting the remote Outback and Sydney Harbor in the path of the moon's dark central shadow before it reaches New Zealand's beautiful South Island.

Both eclipses will be spectacular, and both will require careful planning, yet they promise very different experiences. The 2027 event combines over six minutes of totality with some of the very best weather prospects possible, while 2028 offers over five minutes of totality above some of the world's most famous wildernesses and cityscapes.

Eclipse chasing requires careful planning and dedication, but also significant funds. If you can only choose one, which should it be?

On paper, 2027 is difficult to beat. Maximum totality on Aug. 2 will last about 6 minutes, 23 seconds, making it the longest totality on land since 1991 and until 2114. The path of totality will cross southern Spain and Gibraltar before sweeping across Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, Libya, Egypt, Sudan, Saudi Arabia, Yemen, Somalia and the Chagos Islands. About 88.9 million people live in its path, according to Time and Date. It will dominate the news for weeks.

For Europeans, southern Spain is the obvious easy option. Tarifa, at the country's southern tip, will see about 4 minutes, 39 seconds of totality, while the U.K. Overseas Territory of Gibraltar gets about 4 minutes, 25 seconds. Travel farther east and the duration increases, with Sfax in Tunisia getting around 5 minutes, 41 seconds and locations in Egypt experiencing more than six minutes. Weather prospects generally improve, too, as the path crosses the deserts of North Africa.

Egypt is the headline destination. Luxor will see about 6 minutes, 20 seconds of totality near midday, with Karnak Temple, the Valley of the Kings, and some of the world's greatest ancient monuments nearby. The climatic odds are excellent, with clouds extremely rare in early August. That combination of a very long totality, ancient landscapes and a very high probability of a clear sky makes 2027's path of totality highly unusual.

But there are downsides. Temperatures around Luxor can exceed 105°F (41°C) in August, a dust storm is not impossible, and totality occurs shortly after 1 p.m. when the sun (and moon) will be high overhead — making photography very difficult. Demand is already intense, making organized trips expensive. Spain will be considerably easier and probably cheaper for European eclipse chasers, but at the expense of roughly two minutes of totality — and slightly less favorable weather prospects.

If 2027 is about extreme duration, 2028 is about choice. On July 22, 2028, a path of totality will cross the Cocos Islands, Christmas Island, Australia, from northwest to southeast — passing directly over Sydney — before continuing across the Tasman Sea to New Zealand's South Island. That's about 6.3 million people, according to Time and Date. This will be an exclusive eclipse experienced by relatively few people, certainly when compared to the eclipses in 2024, 2026 and 2027.

Maximum totality will last 5 minutes and 10 seconds in the remote Kimberley region of Western Australia. That's more than a minute shorter than 2027, but still exceptionally long by total solar eclipse standards (most last about two minutes). More importantly, the Australian Outback has excellent climatic prospects. Historical cloudiness on July 22 is around 8% at Purnululu (Bungle Bungles) close to the point of greatest eclipse in Western Australia and 19% at Karlu Karlu (Devil's Marbles) in the Northern Territory, making Australia's interior an attractive destination for serious eclipse chasers. Temperatures will be around 86°F (30°C) in July.

Then there's Sydney. Australia's largest city will experience about 3 minutes, 45 seconds of totality, its first total solar eclipse since 1857. Sydney Opera House and Harbor Bridge beneath a totally eclipsed sun could produce some of the decade's defining astronomical images, while millions of people experiencing totality together should create an extraordinary atmosphere. Temperatures will be around 62.6°F (17°C).

A compromise is weather. Historical cloudiness in Sydney is around 43%, which is good odds for most eclipses — and July is known for clear weather. But in 2028, anyone prioritizing their chances of a clear totality will be tempted by a (albeit pricier) trip to the Outback. For Europeans, reaching Australia also comes with considerable cost and time. The huge number of hotels in Sydney could keep accommodation relatively competitive, but the long flight means it makes little sense to travel there for only a few days. For many international eclipse chasers, 2028 will naturally become an expensive one- or two-week trip.

There's another reason to think beyond those few minutes of darkness. With the right planning, an eclipse trip can also become an extraordinary astronomy vacation (tip: come a week before the eclipse for the darkest evening skies). Here, 2028 offers visitors from Europe and North America something very different — the Southern Hemisphere night sky.

July is a superb time to see the bright central regions of the Milky Way from dark locations in Australia. The Southern Cross, or Crux, is one of the southern sky's defining sights, with Alpha and Beta Centauri nearby. Omega Centauri, the largest and brightest globular cluster visible from Earth, is another showpiece, while the Eta Carinae region offers one of the richest sections of the Milky Way for binoculars and small telescopes.

There are other reasons to extend the trip. A partial lunar eclipse occurs on July 6-7, 2028, while the Southern Delta Aquariid meteor shower peaks around July 28 — a week after the eclipse, during a first-quarter moon — and is particularly well seen from the Southern Hemisphere. Add Australia's world-class dark skies, and a trip into the Outback could become as much about stargazing as the eclipse itself.

The 2027 eclipse has fewer night-sky extras. The Delta Aquariid meteor shower peaks a few days before the eclipse — in dark, moonless skies — while Jupiter will dominate the western sky shortly after sunset. However, anyone traveling from the Northern Hemisphere will largely see a familiar celestial hemisphere. Australia offers a genuinely different sky experience.

Perhaps the most useful way to choose between these eclipses is not to compare their durations, but to imagine where you would most like to be when the moon's shadow arrives.

In 2027, the decision largely comes down to how far along the eclipse track you want to travel. Stay in southern Spain for convenience and around four minutes of totality, head into Tunisia for longer totality and excellent weather prospects, or go all-in on Egypt for more than six minutes beneath almost cloudless desert skies — and bragging rights among eclipse chasers. It's an eclipse that can be combined with beaches, Roman ruins, North African cities or the temples and, of course, the tombs of ancient Egypt.

In 2028, the contrast is even greater. Sydney offers a communal total solar eclipse — a busy "we eclipse" — with millions watching daylight disappear above one of the world's great cities. Head thousands of miles away into the Australian interior and the same event becomes a lonely "me eclipse" in the wilderness, with up to five minutes of totality above an immense Outback landscape. Continue to New Zealand, and there's yet another possibility — a shorter totality with the sun much lower in the afternoon sky.

If your priority is purely totality duration, 2027 marginally wins. More than six minutes of totality combined with extraordinarily reliable weather is a rare combination. There's a good reason Aug. 2, 2027 is being marketed as the "eclipse of the century." But if you've always wanted to visit Australia or New Zealand, the 2028 eclipse is an extraordinary excuse to finally go, in addition to experiencing a long totality.

Choose the trip you most want to take, then find the best possible place for you within the path of totality. After all, no total solar eclipse lasts long enough, and most eclipse chasers struggle to recall exactly how long totality lasted. They're just left with the same question as always — when is the next one?

Jamie is an experienced science and travel journalist, stargazer and eclipse chaser who writes about exploring the night sky, solar and lunar eclipses, the Northern Lights, moon-gazing, astro-travel, astronomy and space exploration. He is the editor of WhenIsTheNextEclipse.com, author of A Stargazing Program For Beginners, co-author of The Eclipse Effect, and a senior contributor at Forbes.

#846. Dortmund fans' group criticises Nmecha celebration

Felix Nmecha joined Borussia Dortmund from Wolfsburg in 2023

A Christian group for footballers says it wants to "demonstrate love and respect towards everyone" following criticism from Borussia Dortmund fans of midfielder Felix Nmecha's goal celebration.

A supporters' group said it objected to Nmecha's goal celebration because it referenced a campaign by Ballers in God called 'The King's Return'.

The supporters' group said, external the campaign discriminates against homosexuality and transgender people, paints abortion as "Satan's plan" and is at odds with Dortmund's values of tolerance and respecting diversity.

To celebrate his two goals in the 2-1 win over Elversberg on Saturday, Nmecha pointed to the sky and mimed taking a crown off his head and placing it on the ground.

He said there were "misunderstandings" over his celebration and that it was "not intended to promote myself or any organisation".

Citing a recent investigation by German broadcaster ARD, the fans' group said "extremely conservative positions against homosexuality and transgender identity are advocated" by the campaign.

Ballers in God, external was created by former Crystal Palace and Tottenham midfielder John Bostock.

The organisation promotes Christian beliefs and has high-profile followers such as England's Marc Guehi and Bukayo Saka and former Brazil forward Kaka.

In response to the supporters' group's claims, Ballers in God said: "We are encouraged by player-led movements such as The King's Return, where footballers themselves take the initiative to express their faith in Jesus.

"Our desire is not only to share our hope, but to demonstrate love and respect towards everyone, including those who do not share our beliefs.

"Our focus has always been, and will always be, to point people to Jesus with grace and love."

Nmecha said: "My message has never been about promoting intolerance, discrimination, or hate in any form."

Last year the Premier League withdrew from the Rainbow Laces campaign and ended its partnership with LGBTQ+ charity Stonewall.

In 2024 then Ipswich captain Sam Morsy, a Muslim, said he did not wear a rainbow armband because of his "religious beliefs".

Guehi wrote "I [heart] Jesus" on his rainbow armband when he captained Palace.

Manchester United abandoned plans to wear a jacket supporting the LGBTQ+ community because a player refused.

#845. Hill gets first England call-up as Konsa cover

James Hill has played for England Under-20s and U21s

Bournemouth defender James Hill has been called up to the England squad for the first time.

The 24-year-old centre-back has been added to Thomas Tuchel's squad after Arsenal's Ezri Konsa was ruled out of Thursday's Nations League match against Croatia at Wembley.

Konsa was substituted after sustaining a knee injury in the Champions League win at Slavia Prague on Wednesday, but played all 90 minutes of the win over Hull on Saturday.

He will return to full training this week, before England's game against Spain in Madrid on Sunday.

On Sunday Dan Burn replaced centre-back Marc Guehi, who withdrew with a hip injury.

Hill has played every minute of Bournemouth's Premier League season and has featured in every game of their inaugural Europa League campaign.

He joined Bournemouth from Fleetwood for an undisclosed fee in January 2022.

Having made only 24 appearances in his first three and a half years with the club, Hill became a regular last season as Bournemouth achieved their highest top-flight finish of sixth.

Bournemouth, who are on an eight-match winning run in all competitions, are seventh in the Premier League.

#844. ‘I’ve had to prove people wrong’: Kane still striving before record England cap

Captain to surpass Shilton with 126th cap against Croatia

Kane aims to increase record for younger players to catch

Harry Kane says he still feels a pressure to prove his worth, even as he prepares to become England’s most capped men’s player, as he outlined his determination to set records that will stand for years.

The captain will make his 126th appearance against Croatia at ­Wembley on Thursday night, moving him ahead of Peter Shilton on the all-time list. Kane is England’s record ­goalscorer with 91, comfortably clear of Wayne Rooney, who retired with 53.

Kane will be presented with a memento of his historic cap by ­Shilton before kick-off against ­Croatia. ­Shilton has held the record since 1990 when he finished his 20-year career. Kane’s achievement of winning the Ballon d’Or last month will also be recognised.

“I don’t think it will ever leave me,” Kane said, when asked whether he continued to have points to prove. “It’s probably part of what makes me push myself to the limits that I do because in football, you’ve never completed it. No matter what you’ve achieved, there is always a trophy that someone else has won or a goal record that someone else has.

“Whether it’s noise from the outside, from media or the fans … it just helps motivate me to realise there’s a lot more to achieve. My biggest fear is finishing my career and thinking I could have done a bit more … if I could have just done that or done that. I want to make sure I cross every bridge and do everything possible so that whenever that day does come, I can say I’ve done everything possible. And I can sleep well at night.”

The 33-year-old is conscious that two of his England teammates have won a significant number of caps. Declan Rice has 80 at the age of 27; Jude Bellingham 60 at 23. “I’ll try to give them a good number to catch,” Kane said. “The goal record, of course, is going to be one that’s difficult to beat for a while.

“I’ve spoken about leading by example and pushing a lot of these younger players. It’s by setting standards, being available every time, getting the caps and scoring the goals. That should help motivate the younger players. If I was younger and I had a player in front of me doing what I was doing, I know that would push me to think: ‘OK, I can score those goals, I can win the Ballon d’Or, I can break the cap record.’ Whilst I’m in this place, it is to try to set these records as high as I can and one day look back to see if anyone can catch them.”

Kane has been doubted at ­numerous points of his career, ­starting when he was released by Arsenal as an eight-year-old. He had difficult loans from Tottenham to Norwich and Leicester in 2012‑13 and there were the one‑season‑wonder jibes after his breakthrough campaign for Spurs and England in 2014-15.

Kane has been ridiculed for ­setting lofty targets: such as in 2017, when he said he wanted to replicate the numbers of Lionel Messi and ­Cristiano Ronaldo; when he stated his ambition to win the 2018 World Cup Golden Boot. Or when he stood on the verge of his 100th England cap in September 2024 with 66 goals and said he wanted to score 100. There were questions about his place in the team after Euro 2024 when his performances were underwhelming and he was substituted in the final. Every time, he answered back.

“It’s just my mindset,” Kane said. “Because I’ve had to prove people wrong my whole career. From early academy days proving coaches wrong, proving scouts wrong – it has just been instilled in me. If someone tells me I can’t do something it motivates me more to do it.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

“When you look at all the great athletes, I’ve spoken before about Tom Brady [the NFL icon] and it’s that unwavering mentality to be the best. Maybe with me, because I’m a calm person and you don’t see … like, the ego of some of these great players and I’m a bit more relaxed … but it doesn’t mean I don’t want it as much as everyone else. That I don’t put in the work and drive myself and everyone around me to be the best.

“Maybe getting released that early [by Arsenal] and ­proving them wrong and then maybe ­proving [wrong] my early coaches at ­Tottenham, who I wasn’t playing as much [under]. The loan moves that didn’t go well. Same thing: ‘I’m going to show them.’”

Kane brought up surely the lowest individual moment of his England career – the penalty miss against France in the 2-1 World Cup ­quarter‑final defeat in 2022. “That was really tough but again it was the way I bounced back,” he said.

“And even the fact I scored the next 30 [actually 31] penalties of my career. I changed the technique a little bit and it made me improve. There have been a lot of low points but maybe they are things that have helped me get to where I am now.”

#843. How Germany's greatest goalscorer is guiding the next generation

Miroslav Klose's FC Nuremberg side sit second in the 2. Bundesliga

It is no surprise Miroslav Klose recognises the value of a true goalscorer.

He is, after all, Germany's all-time leading marksman and until this summer had netted more than any other player in men's World Cup history. Even now, only Kylian Mbappe and Lionel Messi can top his 16 across four tournaments.

But of the more than 300 goals Klose scored in a career that began in Germany's amateur leagues and spanned Kaiserslautern, Werder Bremen, Bayern Munich and Lazio, he reckons all but two came inside the penalty area.

"Thankfully, we've moved away a little from the idea of the false nine or having a second striker playing around the main striker, with everyone coming towards the ball," explains the FC Nuremberg boss.

"For me, the most important thing is that you need someone who is there to score goals. You need someone in the box because that's where you're closest to the goal. That's why I'm a big believer in practising the final ball, whether it's a cross, a shot or something else.

"That's crucial. How do you create that final ball? When you develop automatisms and players get to know each other better, that's when you see harmony on the pitch.

"It can make things look effortless, but it involves a huge amount of work. A lot of work in training and attention to detail, making sure the players communicate with each other and understand their team-mates' strengths and weaknesses."

That focus on detail stems from Klose's diligence during his playing days. He would study opponents' movement, analyse a goalkeeper's position and shape when facing certain shots - do they make themselves big? Are their hands high or low?

"When goals are scored, the whole team deserves credit," adds the 48-year-old, who was as selfless as he was ruthless. "But you still need someone who has that ability in their feet or in their head to put the ball in the net."

"He's a great role model for me" - Former German forward on Harry Kane

Klose was 36 when he won the World Cup with Germany in 2014 - surpassing Ronaldo's goal record in a 7-1 semi-final thrashing of hosts Brazil.

It was the culmination of a career built on hard work after a series of near-misses - something that may offer solace to Harry Kane and England that a major tournament triumph remains possible.

Born in communist Poland, Klose's father Josef - also a footballer, most notably for Auxerre - moved the family to West Germany when his son was eight.

He was never in a big academy, playing in the lower leagues while training as a carpenter before eventually joining Kaiserslautern.

Klose, like Kane, was in his early 20s by the time he established himself in top-flight football, but just two years after his Bundesliga debut was starting a World Cup final defeat by Brazil.

The striker, 38 when he hung up his goalscoring boots, admires the way Kane has evolved as he has matured, using him as an example to his own young prospects.

"You could always see his quality, and he's worked incredibly hard to get where he is," says Klose of the Ballon d'Or winner.

"He's also a great role model for me, particularly because he has stayed in Germany. I often tell my players that they should look at someone like him as an example.

"Young players can't yet have the instinct and experience he has developed, but that's where it starts - thinking about what you can and can't do as a footballer. You have to keep learning. That's the crucial thing for me.

"If you understand that you train to become better, then in five years' time you'll naturally be a different player. But if you think everything will happen automatically just because 10 people around you tell you that you're a fantastic player, I don't think you'll continue to develop."

Klose's Nuremberg have the youngest average age in the 2. Bundesliga

Klose has a knack for working with young talent, previously coaching Bayern Munich's under-17s. His Nuremberg side are the youngest in the German second tier with an average age of 23.3 years, according to Transfermarkt.

"You need that balance and a certain core of experienced players," he explains. "But we're very brave in that respect. Over the three years I've been here, we've made progress in how we assess young players and in the conversations we have about them.

"How do we rate them? How far along are they? What do they need to work on to take the next step? Is it perhaps more about their physical development? Because from a footballing perspective, we're already producing some really good players."

Klose's coaching journey began with the national team before he joined Bayern, briefly becoming Hansi Flick's assistant, and then took his first managerial role at Rheindorf Altach in Austria.

He joined Nuremberg, historically one of Germany's most successful clubs, in 2024 and steered them to 10th and eighth-placed finishes.

This season they sit second, behind Hertha BSC, and are the league's joint-top scorers, with eyes on a return to the Bundesliga for the first time since 2019.

"When I first arrived, I spoke to the youth coaches about the club's DNA and its coaching philosophy, and what they focus on," adds Klose.

"There was already a lot of common ground. We suggested trying certain things because we wanted to do a little more in particular areas, and they were open to that.

"That's important. We benefit from this because our young players are getting opportunities in the first team, and everyone is paying attention to their development.

"But that journey starts with the youth coaches. I know how important it is to take those steps. We're benefiting from that now because we have access to so many young talents.

"As a coaching team, we're brave enough to give them opportunities when we see that they can compete at this level. That's the first step."

Among the 11 to play the most minutes for Klose's side this season, seven are 22 years old or under, including top scorer Mohamed Ali Zoma, already capped by Italy.

"Of course, everyone gets a lot of praise, as is currently the case with Marc Kornwachs," says Klose of a 17-year-old midfielder also catching the eye.

"But his journey isn't over yet. Now it's about helping him become more consistent and establishing himself, while continuing to develop his game and take further steps forward.

"These players are so talented that we have absolutely no hesitation in giving them opportunities, regardless of the scoreline."

Klose was still playing fifth-tier amateur football aged 20 before becoming the World Cup's all-time top goalscorer in 2014

Klose also understands his managerial career is still young - mirroring the humble nature that earned him fair play awards in Germany and Italy.

"I'm very comfortable with the steps I've taken, even though it involves a huge amount of work," he says about his progress. "You learn something every day.

"I've said that I'm already a much better manager than I was three years ago. That's perfectly normal, and you have to embrace it. I've always been willing and eager to learn, and I've always been a hard worker. That isn't going to change."

So what does a Miroslav Klose team look like?

"Personally, as a player, I always liked having the ball for long periods, and that hasn't changed," he explains.

"When you have the ball, you have a certain level of dominance. I know you also have to be very adaptable in terms of possession, and that's something we are. We constantly show the players different ways of playing out of situations.

"It's great to see how they develop and to be able to support individual players along the way. That's exactly the approach I like to take as a manager."

#842. Gene editing could replace a lifetime of medication, but there's a catch

Imagine receiving a single treatment that could keep your cholesterol under control for decades, potentially eliminating the need for daily medication. Advances in gene editing are bringing that possibility closer to reality. But scientists say the same technology that could revolutionize medicine also raises difficult questions about safety, permanent genetic changes, and unintended consequences.

Gene therapy is already being used to treat certain serious illnesses. These treatments can introduce working copies of genes, silence harmful genetic activity, or make changes directly to DNA. Unlike conventional medications that must be taken repeatedly, some genetic treatments are designed to work after just one administration.

More than 6,000 rare genetic disorders have been identified, although only a small proportion currently have targets that can be treated. Gene therapies have already achieved important successes against conditions such as spinal muscular atrophy and sickle cell disease.

Now, researchers are exploring whether similar approaches could help prevent or manage far more widespread health problems, including high cholesterol, heart disease, obesity, and diabetes.

That raises a fundamental question: Just because scientists can permanently change a person's genetic activity, does that mean they should?

In a perspective published in JAMA Internal Medicine, University of Michigan Health Frankel Cardiovascular Center cardiologists Eric D. Smith, M.D., and Venkatesh L. Murthy, M.D., Ph.D., outline how doctors and researchers should weigh the potential benefits of genomic therapies against their risks.

The two gene therapy researchers explain why these treatments are so promising, what makes them different from conventional medicines, and what must happen before they can be safely offered to millions of people.

Why One-Time Gene Therapy Is Different From Daily Medication

One of the most appealing features of gene therapy is the possibility of achieving lasting results without repeated treatments.

Traditional medicines generally work only as long as patients continue taking them. Genomic therapies operate differently because they act on genetic material itself. They may provide a healthy version of a gene, suppress a gene responsible for harmful effects, or modify a specific DNA sequence.

This makes it possible to develop treatments intended to work after a single dose. Such therapies are often called "one-and-done" treatments.

However, receiving a treatment only once does not necessarily mean its effects will last a lifetime.

Smith explains that many gene therapies use modified viruses to carry genetic instructions into cells. The immune system can recognize these delivery vehicles and develop a response against them. As a result, administering the same treatment again may be difficult or impossible, even if its benefits begin to fade.

Another important distinction concerns which cells are changed. Current gene therapies generally target somatic cells, which are the body's cells other than those involved in reproduction. Unlike germline editing, these treatments are not intended to create genetic changes that can be inherited by future generations.

Why Gene Editing Common Diseases Raises New Risks

For people living with rare, devastating genetic conditions, the benefits of gene therapy may clearly outweigh the potential dangers. Some patients have few effective treatment options, making even an experimental intervention worth considering.

The situation becomes considerably more complicated when the same technology is used against common diseases.

Conditions such as high cholesterol, heart disease, obesity, and diabetes already have established treatments. Many of these medications can be adjusted as a patient's condition changes or discontinued if troublesome side effects develop.

A permanent genetic intervention may not offer that flexibility.

Murthy also points to a major concern involving the number of people who might eventually receive these treatments. A serious side effect that occurs only rarely could still harm a substantial number of patients if a therapy is administered to millions.

For that reason, treatments intended for widespread use must meet especially demanding safety standards.

Five Questions Scientists Say Must Be Answered

To help determine when genomic therapy is appropriate, Smith and Murthy propose evaluating five essential factors:

The final question may be especially challenging.

Clinical trials typically involve relatively small groups of patients who are monitored for limited periods. Although these studies can identify many important safety concerns, they may miss extremely rare complications or problems that take years to develop.

Some adverse effects might only become apparent after a treatment has reached a much larger population.

The Problem of Tracking Risks That Could Emerge Years Later

Smith argues that long-term monitoring cannot be treated as an afterthought. It needs to be an essential part of how gene therapies are introduced into medical practice.

Patient registries, which collect information about people receiving particular treatments, have already shown how valuable extended follow-up can be.

However, therapies that could eventually reach millions of patients will require monitoring systems capable of operating on a much larger scale.

These systems must be independent and standardized so researchers can consistently evaluate whether treatments remain effective and whether unexpected health problems appear over time.

Without reliable long-term data, doctors may struggle to determine the full consequences of genetic interventions that cannot easily be reversed.

Could Some Genetic Changes Be Too Risky to Make Permanent?

Another concern is whether certain diseases or biological processes are suitable for permanent treatment at all.

Murthy emphasizes that developing the ability to alter a genetic target does not automatically make doing so the best medical decision.

Some conditions require careful adjustments to medication doses over time. In other cases, the difference between an effective treatment and a harmful one can be extremely small. Changing a biological process too much or too little could create serious complications.

Conventional medications offer an important advantage in these situations because doctors can modify or stop treatment as needed.

Permanent gene therapies generally lack that option.

Scientists may eventually overcome this limitation by developing genetic treatments with built-in biological "off-switches" or other methods for reversing their effects.

Until those approaches have been shown to work reliably, the ability to undo or adjust a treatment remains an important safety advantage of traditional medicine.

The Million-Dollar Challenge Facing Gene Therapy

Safety is not the only barrier to bringing gene editing into mainstream healthcare. Cost could also determine whether these treatments become widely available.

Some existing gene therapies have list prices above $1 million for a single patient, and several cost substantially more.

Such prices may be considered justifiable for certain rare, life-threatening conditions, particularly when treatment options are extremely limited.

But applying similar pricing to diseases affecting millions of people would place enormous financial pressure on healthcare systems.

Smith and Murthy argue that affordability and access must therefore be part of the discussion from the beginning.

Even a highly effective gene therapy could create new healthcare inequalities if only a small percentage of patients could obtain it. Researchers and policymakers must consider not just whether these treatments work, but also whether they can be delivered without making existing disparities worse.

Could One Gene-Editing Treatment Prevent Heart Disease for Decades?

Despite these challenges, the possibility of using gene editing to prevent common diseases is becoming increasingly realistic.

Researchers are already conducting early studies to investigate whether a single genetic treatment can produce long-lasting reductions in LDL, commonly known as "bad," cholesterol.

LDL cholesterol contributes to the buildup of fatty deposits inside arteries, which can increase the risk of heart attacks and other cardiovascular problems. Lowering LDL over extended periods is an important strategy for reducing cardiovascular risk.

If gene editing can safely produce sustained reductions, it could eventually offer a new approach to protecting cardiovascular health without requiring patients to take medication indefinitely.

However, promising early results will not be enough to justify widespread use.

Before these therapies become routine options for common conditions, researchers will need convincing evidence that their benefits last, their risks remain acceptably low over many years, and their costs are manageable. Reliable safeguards will also be essential.

For Smith and Murthy, the objective is not to hold back genetic medicine. It is to make sure that a technology with the potential to transform healthcare is introduced carefully and responsibly.

As gene therapy moves beyond rare disorders toward conditions affecting millions of people, the central challenge will be ensuring that the promise of lasting protection does not come at the expense of long-term patient safety.

#841. Danny Kelly, football broadcaster and renowned editor, dies aged 69

Danny Baker pays tribute to the ‘funniest man I knew’

Kelly was former editor of the NME and Q magazines

The journalist and broadcaster Danny Kelly, who helped define coverage of music and football in the UK for a generation, has died at the age of 69.

Kelly edited the NME and Q magazine, and launched the Football 365 website before going on to be a presenter and pundit on the BBC and TalkSport. He had been receiving treatment for oesophageal cancer.

Tributes were led by Kelly’s longstanding broadcast partner Danny Baker. “My great friend, supreme broadcaster and funniest man I ever knew, Danny Kelly, died yesterday afternoon,” Baker wrote on social media, the pair having worked together on any number of radio, TV shows and podcasts. “I cannot believe I will never hear his voice again.”

Tottenham Hotspur paid emotional tribute to Kelly, a lifelong Spurs fan. A statement said: “The entire Tottenham family mourns the loss of one of our own, broadcasting legend Danny Kelly. Our thoughts and love are with his family and friends at this incredibly sad time.”

TalkSport, for which Kelly worked as a presenter for nearly two decades, said it was “heartbroken” by the news. “A cherished part of TalkSport for so many years, Danny brought extraordinary wit, warmth and knowledge to our airwaves,” the station said. “His passion for football, music and life was infectious, and his kindness touched everyone around him.”

Another broadcaster, the former Sky Sports host Richard Keys, said Kelly “was all of the things – and more – being said about him – ‘warm, witty and knowledgable’”.

Kelly was born in north London in 1956 and first made his name writing about music. He began contributing to the NME in his 20s and went on to edit the agenda-setting weekly newspaper at the end of the 1980s. From there he took charge of the top-selling music monthly Q magazine, where he was named British magazine editor of the year.

Manic Street Preachers paid tribute to “a brilliant broadcaster-writer-ideas factory. Danny was editor of the NME when we first started getting press, a wonderful man, his musical knowledge was vast and deep, his radio voice has been part of our lives for so long … We will all miss him.”

In the second half of the 1990s, Kelly threw himself into the nascent world of digital media and launched Football365, which became one of the leading online voices on the sport. In the noughties, he spotted another development – podcasts – and launched the Game, a weekly football podcast, for the Times.

Over the past 15 years Kelly became best known as a radio presenter and podcast host, including presenting the Tottenham-focused show View from The Lane. Paying tribute to “our host, our leader” on its X account, the View from the Lane said: “We all loved him as much as he loved Spurs.”

While rivals announce increasingly expensive smart telescopes, ZWO’s new Seestar S30 Plus makes galaxy and nebula photography surprisingly affordable.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

As rival makers announce increasingly ambitious smart telescopes, ZWO has taken a different approach. Its new Seestar S30 Plus launched today and is available for $474 from Seestar’s website and Amazon, just in time for Christmas. Better still, we’ve been using it for a month and can bring you a first look.

Announced a few months after the flagship Seestar S50 Pro and replacing the now-discontinued Seestar S30, the new Seestar S30 Plus retains its 30mm aperture and compact chassis, but upgrades to four-element apochromatic optics with extra-low dispersion (ED) glass and two 3.7-megapixel cameras.

It has a 1.2-inch (30 mm) aperture, two 3.7 MP cameras and four-element apochromatic optics bundled into a compact build.

Both produce 1,440 x 2,560-pixel images, while a much-improved 43.5-degree wide-angle camera can capture the Milky Way, constellations, star trails and nightscapes. Built-in filters, a mosaic mode and equatorial (EQ) tracking add considerable deep-sky astrophotography potential.

For a telescope weighing just 3.64 lbs (1.65 kg), it’s impressive. It easily fits into a camera bag and could happily live on a bookshelf.

I’ve already photographed the Andromeda Galaxy (M31), the Pleiades (M45), the Dumbbell Nebula (M27) and the North America Nebula (NGC 7000). The results are excellent for such a small instrument, especially when imaging nebulas with its built-in dual-band filter, which helps reduce light pollution.

The Seestar app adds new in-app post-processing options, so you don’t have to mess around with any of that — though you can also export everything as lossless FITS files. The S30 Plus also includes a magnetic solar filter, enabling you to indulge in solar photography safely.

With Dwarflab’s $1,299 Draco (3.5-inch/90mm aperture) recently landed in stores and Vaonis’ own $4,990 Atlas (3.1-inch/80mm aperture) not available until 2027, ZWO’s decision to offer an upgraded entry-level smart telescope that buyers can get their hands on right now looks particularly smart.

With ZWO's pattern of delivering cheaper smart telescopes without sacrificing on quality, the Seestar S30 Plus could be one of Christmas 2026’s best gifts for anyone interested in astronomy — and maybe that’s the point of it. Either way, first impressions are good. A full review is coming tomorrow, so check back at Space.com to find out our full thoughts and testing.

#839. The brain’s hidden fear mechanism may explain anxiety and PTSD

The brain has a remarkable ability to recognize danger, but new research suggests that this survival mechanism may also explain why people sometimes feel threatened in situations that are actually safe. The discovery offers a possible explanation for the intense fear responses associated with anxiety and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD).

For years, scientists believed that fear helps the brain distinguish more clearly between threatening and harmless experiences. However, a study led by researchers at the Douglas Research Centre at McGill University and the University of Toronto-Scarborough challenges that assumption. The findings, published in Nature Neuroscience, suggest that fear may have the opposite effect.

In experiments involving mice, researchers trained the animals to associate one environment with danger and another with safety. Instead of developing increasingly separate neural representations of the two locations, the animals' brain activity began to show overlapping patterns. In other words, the brain's representations of safe and dangerous experiences became less distinct.

"Our findings suggest fear may blur the boundary between danger and safety rather than sharpen it," said senior author Mark Brandon, Associate Professor in McGill's Department of Psychiatry and Researcher at the Douglas. "This could reshape how scientists think about anxiety and PTSD."

How Scientists Watched the Brain Process Fear

To investigate how these changes occur, the research team developed an unusual experimental setup that combined augmented reality with real-time brain imaging.

The researchers created a specialized arena in which mice could be virtually "teleported" between environments associated with danger and safety. By changing the sights and sounds surrounding the animals, scientists could make them experience different settings without physically moving them to another location.

At the same time, miniature microscopes monitored hundreds of neurons in the hippocampus, a brain region essential for learning and memory. This allowed the team to observe how the brain's activity changed as the mice transitioned between experiences associated with safety and threat.

"That gave us something conventional fear conditioning experiments cannot easily provide: a moment-by-moment view of the brain switching between competing maps of dangerous and safe memories," said Robert Rozeske, Assistant Professor in University of Toronto's Department of Psychology and lead author on the publication.

Why the Brain May Confuse Safety With Danger

Although mixing memories of safe and dangerous experiences might seem like a problem, the researchers believe it could serve an important evolutionary purpose.

The experiments suggested that overlapping memory representations allowed the brain to retrieve information about previous threats more rapidly. This could help an animal recognize possible danger and respond before it is too late.

Such a strategy comes with a trade-off. By prioritizing speed over accuracy, the brain may react to a potential threat even when the current situation is harmless. From a survival perspective, responding unnecessarily to a false alarm may sometimes be preferable to overlooking a genuine danger.

"The ventral hippocampus may be part of a system that prioritizes a rapid 'better safe than sorry' response," said Rozeske. "In other words, the brain may sacrifice precision for speed when danger matters."

The ventral hippocampus is a part of the hippocampus involved in processing emotionally significant experiences, including fear and anxiety. The new findings suggest that overlapping memory representations in this region may help the brain switch rapidly into a defensive state.

A Hidden Survival Mechanism May Help Explain PTSD

The discovery could also offer insight into why people with anxiety and trauma-related disorders sometimes experience powerful fear responses in situations that pose no immediate threat.

For someone with PTSD, an otherwise harmless sight, sound, or environment can trigger memories associated with a traumatic experience. The resulting fear can feel immediate and overwhelming, even when the person is objectively safe.

The researchers suggest that such reactions may arise, at least in part, when a normally useful survival mechanism becomes excessively sensitive. Instead of reflecting a system that has simply stopped distinguishing between different memories, these responses might involve a brain mechanism that shifts too quickly from recognizing safety to anticipating danger.

"Our study suggests that's not necessarily a broken pattern-separation system, but possibly an overactive version of a normal survival mechanism gone into overdrive," said Brandon. "That reframing could guide therapeutic approaches to address an overly fast transition to 'danger mode'."

Because the experiments were conducted in mice, additional research is needed to determine whether the same mechanisms contribute to anxiety and PTSD in humans. Nevertheless, the findings provide a new way to understand how fear influences memory and why a brain system designed to protect against danger might sometimes generate fear when no immediate threat exists.

The study, "Overlapping representations in the ventral hippocampus support rapid fear memory retrieval," by Robert Rozeske and Mark Brandon, was published in Nature Neuroscience.

The research received support from the Canadian Institutes of Health Research and the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada.
