At the height of the Cold War, two amateur radio operators alleged they intercepted signals from Soviet cosmonauts who perished during missions that remained secret.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In the final weeks of 1960, two young radio enthusiasts were monitoring transmissions from a home-built listening station on a rooftop in Turin, Italy, when the brothers detected something extraordinary: a faint signal that bore the hallmarks of one originating from space. That wasn't the only surprising thing about the alleged signal:, the transmission carried a very familiar message: it was Morse code for the international distress signal SOS.

As the youths listened, the signal seemed to grow weaker. This raised a troubling possibility: could it be that the signal's source was moving farther away from Earth? And if so, was it possible that this concerning signal was of Soviet origin — perhaps a spacecraft drifting helplessly into space, carrying a cosmonaut on board whose doomed mission had never been publicly acknowledged?

These strange events from November 1960 became the first in a series of alleged radio signal interceptions that would form the basis of an enduring Cold War-era mystery involving so-called "lost cosmonauts" — early Soviet space travelers rumored to have died during secret spaceflight missions before Yuri Gagarin's historic flight the following spring, in April 1961.Today, more than six decades later, the story remains one of the most haunting legends of the Space Age. Were there truly early Soviet space missions — with tragically ill-fated cosmonaut crews — that remain undisclosed to this day?

The peculiar story began in October 1957, as the Italian brothers Achille and Gian Battista Judica-Cordiglia learned, along with the rest of the world, about the Soviet Union's successful launch of Sputnik 1, Earth's first artificial satellite.

Immediately, the two became fascinated with the idea of trying to listen in on signals from such spacecraft and began working to assemble their very own radio tracking station, which they put together mostly from secondhand military surplus equipment. What they couldn't easily find and purchase, the brothers would often assemble themselves. They built an improvised tracking station in an abandoned World War Two bunker, which the brothers dubbed Torre Bert, that eventually became a fully functional radio facility with an antenna they built from salvaged materials like chicken wire and scraps of metal.

Whatever it lacked in aesthetics, the station made up for in functionality, and soon the brothers' amateur efforts reportedly allowed them to successfully intercept transmissions associated with Sputnik 2, the first Soviet spacecraft to carry a living creature into orbit: a dog named Laika, who became a one-way passenger on the mission. Later, the boys also said they were able to track transmissions from America's Explorer 1 satellite.

Some of what the Judica-Cordiglia brothers were able to achieve could be chalked up to being in the right place at the right time. Specifically, their location in northern Italy was advantageous, since it allowed them to monitor signals from Soviet spacecraft passing overhead.

By late November 1960, the Judica-Cordiglia brothers learned of reports from a West German observatory suggesting there may have been an unidentified satellite in orbit, raising an intriguing possibility: could there have been a spacecraft launch that had not been disclosed to the public?

Intrigued, the brothers began spending their evenings at Torre Bert scanning the skies for radio frequencies in search of the alleged mystery object. Eventually, they claimed to have detected a signal that differed significantly from those they had tracked in the past. Unlike the familiar electronic beeps they had intercepted from other satellites, this transmission seemed unmistakable: it was Morse code for SOS.

According to their account, as the pair listened to the alarming transmission, the signal gradually began to fade, raising a disconcerting possibility: what if the spacecraft they were monitoring hadn't merely been traveling through orbit, but had been drifting away from Earth?

If correct, the implications were staggering: the Soviet Union may have launched a secret space mission, but this time with a human cosmonaut on board — and something had gone terribly wrong, ending with a spacecraft and its occupant becoming lost in space.

Significantly, the brothers appear to have reached this conclusion independently, and no verified evidence has ever surfaced establishing that the transmission they claimed to have intercepted originated from a crewed spacecraft, let alone one associated with an unacknowledged Soviet mission that somehow escaped Earth's gravitational influence, with tragic results.

Nonetheless, the brothers' claims would soon help give rise to a disturbing possibility: that there had been unknown "lost" cosmonauts who perished during missions that remained hidden from public knowledge.

The alleged distress signal was only the beginning of a series of unsubstantiated claims the Judica-Cordiglia brothers made, and by the first days of February 1961, the amateur radio sleuths would claim to have intercepted another odd signal. This time, the pair claimed to have heard labored breathing coming across the airwaves, and even what resembled the strained moans of a person aboard an orbiting spacecraft.

In an equally eerie recording the brothers produced, what sounded like a rapidly beating human heart could be heard. The brothers shared the recording with Italian cardiologist Achille Dogliotti, whose examination reportedly led him to conclude that the sounds were consistent with strained breathing and an elevated human heartbeat.

With time, more recordings would begin to appear, featuring transmissions the boys believed to be evidence of unsuccessful Soviet missions that preceded the successful spaceflight of Yuri Gagarin, whose 108-minute journey around Earth in 1961 made him the first human to travel into space.

However, what may be the brothers' most controversial claim involved a recording they believed captured the final moments of a female cosmonaut whose ill-fated journey allegedly occurred prior to the historic 1963 spaceflight of Valentina Tereshkova, the first woman to travel into space. However, experts have pointed out that these transmissions do not follow typical military communications protocols, further casting doubt on their legitimacy.

As the Judica-Cordiglia brothers' notoriety increased, journalists and curiosity-seekers weren't the only ones whose attention they reportedly began to attract; their activities also allegedly garnered interest from intelligence officials.

In one instance, the brothers claimed a man identifying himself as a Russian reporter had visited them. Shortly thereafter, another individual — this time claiming to be an Italian counterintelligence agent — warned them that the "journalist" who had come to see them was a KGB agent.

The Judica-Cordiglias and their unconventional hobby, it seemed, had now placed them in the crosshairs of Soviet intelligence officials.

An unusual twist in this part of the Italian brothers' story would eventually emerge decades later, when London-based journalist Kris Hollington began reinvestigating their claims for a feature story that appeared in the paranormal-focused magazine Fortean Times. According to Hollington, a former Soviet KGB operative who later served as a Russian ambassador to a European country had reportedly confirmed (on condition of anonymity) that Moscow was indeed interested in the Judica-Cordiglias and their claims.

"Our cosmonauts were warned to be careful what they said while in space after this and we had the brothers followed," the former KGB agent reportedly told Hollington.

Things could have ended tragically for the brothers if it were not for the fame they achieved at the time for their alleged radio interceptions. As the former KGB agent told Hollington, it was believed for a time that the brothers "had to be dealt with — an accident perhaps," although after they appeared on a television program that brought them significant attention, any Soviet plans that would have endangered the brothers became impractical.

"That saved their lives," the former KGB agent reportedly told Hollington, who expressed gratitude for the circumstances that may well have saved the Italian brothers, with the former agent confiding to Hollington that he thought "they were good kids."

Of course, the claims of alleged Soviet surveillance are difficult to verify given the anonymity requested by Hollington's source. The same must be said of many of the claims made by the Judica-Cordiglias — even if the brothers were successful in intercepting Soviet transmissions at the time, that alone does not prove that they uncovered evidence of unacknowledged missions during which cosmonauts may have perished.

Some, like spaceflight researcher Sven Grahn, have acknowledged the genuine tracking capabilities the brothers possessed while remaining skeptical of the more sensational "lost cosmonaut" claims, suggesting the brothers might have misinterpreted some of the transmissions they recorded.

"I think that the Judica-Cordiglia brothers did run a tracking station and picked up signals from various spacecraft," Grahn said in an assessment of the brothers and their claims. "However, for some reason they thought that they needed sensational stories [to] maintain their image of a 'hot-shot' operation," he adds. "Once they over-interpreted some receptions and made fantastic claims they were 'trapped' and had to continue to produce sensations."

There is also the possibility that the recordings were hoaxes, of course. Whatever the case, there are no independently verified launch records, authenticated communications, or other evidence from the period that provides additional support for what the brothers claimed to have intercepted.

Something that can be verified, however, is the Soviet Union's well-documented secrecy, adding a further layer of complication to matters. As space historian James Oberg has observed, there are verified instances in which Soviet officials altered photographs and records from the early years of human spaceflight, a fact that has perhaps helped fuel rumors about alleged missing cosmonauts. It is also known that the Soviet space program covered up several deadly disasters, such as a launch pad explosion on Oct. 24, 1960 that killed a high-ranking Soviet military officer and at least 100 others. At the time, Soviet state news outlets reported it as a plane crash.

No verified evidence has emerged to support claims of failed, unacknowledged Soviet crewed spaceflights of the kind described in the lost-cosmonaut legends. Yet the Judica-Cordiglia brothers' accounts have drawn attention for decades and remain among the strangest stories in the lore of the early Space Age — a fact that illustrates humanity's enduring fascination with Cold War mysteries and phenomena that exist beyond Earth.

#815. From Jersey to Somalia... via Liverpool & Man City

Somalia midfielder Jarma Mohamed moved to eighth-tier Jersey Bulls in the summer

Not many 21-year-olds can say they have played international football, had spells at Liverpool and Manchester City and are now playing in non-league after being spotted on a mobile app.

But Jarma Mohamed's footballing journey is not that of your typical midfielder.

The combative playmaker has been recalled to Somalia's side for their 2027 Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) qualifiers with Ghana this month, capping a rollercoaster year for the Liverpudlian.

"My mum was probably fed up with me just booting stuff in the house, so she got me involved as early as I could," Mohamed jokes with BBC Sport as he talks about the start of his footballing journey.

"When I was three she was begging teams to take me because the age that you're allowed is four.

"Eventually someone saw me playing and it turned out to be an Everton scout, so I ended up playing for Everton from four and then at that age between four to nine you can play for a few teams.

"It was at Liverpool and Everton, eventually chose Liverpool at nine, then signed for Man City at 11.

"I came out of Man City and got a scholarship at Wigan, which is one of the best memories of playing football, having a two-year deal, playing day-in, day-out, full-time schedule, staying in digs up in Wigan, travelling up and down the country for away games, performing, picking up the armband a few times, FA Youth Cup, things like that."

Jersey Bulls' midfielder Mohamed wins historic call-up

Jersey Bulls sign Somalia midfielder Mohamed

Mohamed featured alongside players including Jayden Danns at Liverpool and England stars Rico Lewis and Nico O'Reilly at Manchester City.

He was released by Wigan in 2024 and spent time in non-league football with Bamber Bridge and Newcastle Town.

His career came to a crossroads in the summer, when Isthmian League South Central side Jersey Bulls spotted him on an app for footballers.

"I was thinking what do I want to do?," he said.

"I could go abroad and do something, but I wasn't really too sure and I'd been playing showcase games with a company called Player, who basically put players in front of teams, they have an app, which is like a LinkedIn for footballers.

"Jersey Bulls were on the app looking for players and, long story short, the owner of Player put me in contact with Jersey Bulls.

"I know the club's amateur and no-one gets paid, but we worked out a job that aligns with the things that I do, obviously me having Uefa C licence coaching is something that I'd easily do and I've come over and done it."

Jarma Mohamed and his Jersey Bulls team-mates have yet to lose a league game this season

Mohamed now works as a youth coach in the island, while also anchoring the midfield of a Jersey Bulls side riding high in the eighth tier of English football.

Born in Toxteth, Mohamed's Somalian grandfather moved to Liverpool, part of a large Somali community in the city.

It is that heritage that has allowed him to play for a side ranked 200th in the world - the lowest of any team to progress to Afcon 2027's final round of qualifiers.

He made his Somalia debut against Mauritius in March as the Ocean Stars reached the final qualifying stages for Afcon for the first time in their history - they beat the island nation on penalties after two goalless draws.

"It was a random Wednesday afternoon in my kitchen and I was made up," Mohamed says of the moment he was asked to first join the Somalia squad earlier this year.

"I could physically see the community close to home, and going out to the camp and experiencing what that's like, it really lit a fire that I didn't even know I could get as far as trying to push my football career."

He is part of a Somali squad made up of more players from the global diaspora than those born in the country itself.

Having reached the qualifying stage for next year's tournament, the lowest ranked side left face a tough group against three-time champions Ivory Coast, The Gambia and Ghana - who have won the tournament four times and drew 0-0 with England in the group stage of this summer's World Cup.

"Everyone's from different parts of the world, you have lads who are Dutch, from Finland, Italy, there's another scouse with me in the team," Mohamed said.

"When we're all there, and even lads who are local and playing in the Somali league, everyone's just one family.

"That's one thing which we're really good at, we're together as a team, there's no egos.

"Everyone's just really together and wanting to get results for the country, which I feel is very important."

Somalia were narrowly beaten by the Ivory Coast in September

In their first two qualifying matches Somalia have not let themselves down.

The Gambia scored an 83rd-minute winner to overcome them in their opening game, while an Ivory Coast side boasting Real Madrid's summer signing Yan Diomande, Atalanta's Franck Kessie and former Arsenal winger Nicolas Pepe scored in the 89th minute and the fifth minute of added time to earn a 2-0 win.

It means the Somalis are second from bottom in Group C on goal difference, above a Ghana side who have Kim Bjorkegren in interim charge after the Black Stars lost their opening two matches under Carlos Queiroz.

With the tense security situation in Somalia, the Ocean Stars have played all their qualifiers away from home and will face Ghana in back-to-back matches in Takoradi.

So how will Mohamed, who plays in front of sparse crowds in small grounds in the area south of London, approach facing opponents who ply their trade in the biggest leagues in the world?

"The same way I treat every game, you can only play what's in front of you," he added.

"If you play the name or an occasion you're losing before you've even kicked a ball.

"I just play who's in front of me and keep it at that.

"You know the players' levels, the qualities that they have that you have to respect, but you also have to back yourself.

"You're sharing the same pitch for a reason, it's not by accident."

And can the Ocean Stars make next year's tournament in Kenya, Uganda and Tanzania?

"If you come to do nothing less than that you may as well stay home.

"In the two games we've had previously against Ivory Coast and Gambia we've shown that we can compete.

"If you come to play for the experience or 'we're just happy to be there', then there's no point in coming.

#814. Dancing With the Stars Eliminates Frontrunner Before Semi-Finals

Dancing With the Stars' Jenna Dewan and pro Val Chmerkovskiy became the last season 35 couple to be eliminated before the semi-finals on week nine's Grammy Night.

A frontrunner has fallen out of the competition on Dancing With the Stars.

Jenna Dewan's Nov. 10 performance with pro Val Chmerkovskiy became her last on the show—despite receiving the second-highest scores from the judges on Grammy Night.

For the evening featuring winning hits from music's biggest night, the duo teamed up for a Jazz routine to Janet Jackson’s "All for You," earning 28 out of 30 points. They also won their dance battle against Tatyana Ali and pro Jan Ravnik, which earned Dewan an extra two points.

After revealing the eliminated pair who will not move on to the Nov. 17 semi-finals, cohost Julianne Hough was nearly speechless, saying, "You've made it this far—it's shocking, to say the least."

But even after a controversial season—including a weeklong suspension for Chmerkovskiy over comments to judge Carrie Ann Inaba—Dewan shared how she is taking away positive memories.

"Dancing again, getting to share my joy with my family, who's over here every single night—thank you, my baby—I had a great time," she said, referring to fiancé Steve Kazee. "And I loved getting to share that with the world. Honestly, all love."

Meanwhile, other frontrunners—Paralympian Ezra Frech and pro Daniella Karagach—took the audience back to 2003 with an Argentine tango set to Beyoncé's "Crazy in Love," a single that contributed two Grammys to the artist's record as the award show's all-time champion.

Frech and Karagach's moves were rivaled by Harry Shum Jr. and Jenna Johnson's salsa, as the Grey's Anatomy alum spun his partner around the dance floor to Lady Gaga and Bruno Mars' romantic duet, "Die With a Smile."

It was the final showdown in the ballroom before season 35 headed to the semi-finals. The momentous year has previously said goodbye to Summer House star Ciara Miller, The Bachelor's Tyler Cameron and most recently, Julia Stiles.

"It's been an incredible experience. I pulled things out of myself that I didn't realize were there," the Save The Last Dance star said through tears while standing next to partner Ezra Sosa. "Ezra is just an amazing person. I'm going to be sad not to see him every day."

Yet the Prince & Me star still walked away from the show with an incredible memento: matching ink with her ballroom bestie.

In a tattoo tour shared to TikTok after their Nov. 2 departure, Sosa explained they added eight miniature stars on their wrists, symbolizing "one star for every time we got to dance."

But DWTS has also led to more than just meaningful friendships: The show has also led to many behind-the-scenes romances. Keep reading to learn which dance partners' chemistry needed no choreography.

The season 33 partners dated for about seven months between 2024 and spring 2025.

In April 2025, the fellow DWTS pros kissed on the lips onstage on the final night of the series' 2025 tour during their show-closing duet dance, confirming months of romance rumors.

Showmance or Real Deal: Real deal, as their colleague Ezra Sosa wrote "FINALLY" in response to a fans' video of the pair's smooch.

The former Bachelorette and the Jersey Shore star stoked dating rumors during their time competing against one another on season 31, thanks to their flirtations on social media and coy responses when asked about their possible romance.

"You get to know the other celebrities on Dancing with the Stars," Gabby told E! News in December 2022. "So, we formed a friendship right away and I feel like our senses of humor are really similar. I was so tunnel vision during the competition. I was like, 'I'm here to win' and I didn't have room for anything else. So, we live in different states, but we are having fun. We'll see."

Showmance or Real Deal: Forget GTL, this one was DOA. The pair never ended up officially dating and Gabby debuted her romance with comedian and TV writer Robby Hoffman in August 2023. The pair wed in January 2025.

Months after placing fifth in the 31st season of the dance show, the couple confirmed their romance on Valentine's Day 2023. "My Valentine," the CODA actor captioned a selfie with the choreographer. "Happy Valentine's Day!"

Britt and Daniel then announced their engagement in December 2023 and married in front of a trouple of DWTS pros in August 2025.

While she was partnered with Hayes Grier, the two hit it off during season 21's Switch Up week, with Alek calling her "so hot." After her elimination, Emma spilled that she and Alek had yet to go on a date, saying, "We'll see."

Showmance or Real Deal: Given Alek's tendency to blush and avoid answering questions about his feelings for Emma, telling E! News "no comment!" we think this crush was very real. But Emma danced herself off the market following Skarlatos' 2015 run, so if it was real, it wasn't that real.

The dance pro and Bachelorette alum were romantically linked while competing together on DWTS' season 33 in 2024. However, their offscreen chemistry fizzled out by June 2025 shortly after Jenn returned to Miami to finish her master's degree.

Which bring us to these two. After dating a little on and off since 2011, the pros got engaged live on the show in October 2016, and were married in March 2018. However, in Aug. 2022, E! News confirmed that after four years of marriage, Slater and Farber were going their separate ways.

Showmance or Real Deal? Despite the outcome, they were still the real deal and have remained close friends and cordial co-stars after their split.

"It's not a nightmare at all," Emma exclusively told E! News. "We support each other so much that I want the very best for Sasha. We support each other, very, very truly."

Val and Jenna were dating in 2015, before she was promoted to pro dancer. They got engaged in June of 2018 before making it official and walking down the aisle in April of 2019. In July 2022, they announced they were expecting their first baby together. The two welcomed son Rome Valentin in January 2023.

"Life is awesome," Val told E! News in May 2023. Becoming a dad "definitely elevated my joy for life, my joy for my family, and every day I learn something new being a father."

Showmance or Real Deal? Real deal, y'all!

In December 2020, E! News learned the Selling Sunset star was dating the Dancing With the Stars pro after they had competed separately on season 29.

However, after two months of dating, E! News exclusively confirmed they had called it quits. At the time, a source close to the realtor said, "They had a fun time together but in the end, decided it would be best if they part ways. They are still friendly and cordial. It wasn't a messy breakup, just wasn't the right fit or right timing."

Chrishell has since found love with partner G Flip.

Showmance or Real Deal: We're calling Chrishell and Keo's romance the real deal.

Platonic throughout their seventh-place-finishing 2017 run, the Total Bellas star and the former Dancing With the Stars pro found their way back to each other after her split from John Cena in 2018. Nikki confirmed her relationship with Artem in May 2019, and they got engaged later that year.

The WWE Hall of Famer learned she was expecting soon after their Paris engagement, with them welcoming son Matteo Artemovich Chigvintsev in 2020.

Sadly, though, the pair are no longer partnering up. Nikki filed for divorce in September 2024, two weeks after Artem was arrested on suspicion of domestic violence. Ultimately, the Napa County District Attorney's office announced they decided not to file charges against him "after a thorough review of the criminal investigation and careful evaluation of the evidence presented to the DA’s Office."

Nikki and Artem settled their divorce in November 2024, with her rep noting the two also dropped their "the domestic violence restraining orders against each other in an effort to move on with their lives and effectively co-parent their son."

Model Alexis and relatively new pro Alan flirted up a storm throughout season 27, and Ren had admitted on the show that she had a crush on him. At the time, a source even told E! News that they "really enjoy each other's company" and were "seeing where things go."

Showmance or Real Deal? Largely for the cameras, unfortunately. Multiple outlets reported their split in December 2018, blaming it on long-distance and demanding schedules.

The professional dancers got engaged on Dec. 5, 2015 after dating since 2012. Maks proposed onstage at the SWAY: A Dance Trilogy event in Miami. Six months after welcoming their son Shai, the lovebirds exchanged vows during a lavish ceremony in July 2017. They then welcomed baby Rio in June 2023 and their third son Milan in July 2024.

Showmance or Real Deal: A match made in DWTS heaven!

The partners struck up a romance in season five, but broke up a few months after their shocking exit. Still, Sabrina and Mark remained friendly, with The Cheetah Girls star even returning to the ballroom to cheer for him the following season.

Funnily enough, the duo had gone out on several dates before he even signed up for the show. And while they denied any romance rumors during season 18, that didn't stop them from playing up their chemistry during performances.

Soon after the Shark Tank star announced he was separating from his wife of 14 years Diane Plese, sources confirmed to E! News that he and Kym Johnson, his pro partner from season 20, were dating and "really happy together."

While Robert and Kym at first played coy about the nature of their relationship, that quickly stopped. They were engaged in February 2016, married by June 2016, and welcomed twins in April 2018.

Showmance or Real Deal: Very, very, very real.

Partnered in season three, Karina and Mario quickly struck up a romance, which went on for two years, before they called it off for good in 2008. "The relationship wasn't heading in the right direction," Smirnoff's rep said in a statement, after rumors of infidelity on Lopez's part.

The professional dancers got engaged in 2009 following just six months of dating, shortly after her split from Mario Lopez. Sadly, they called it off later that same year. But the duo remained friendly, even going on vacations together.

Married since 2014, the pros announced the arrival of their daughter Nikita in May 2023.

Daniella shared the happy news by posting a photo and video of Pasha with Nikita to Instagram Stories. She wrote "daddy's girl" alongside the clip and "My Geminis" beside the picture.

After showing off their insane chemistry during the sixth season, the duo dated for nearly a year before announcing their 2009 breakup in the most cordial way ever: matching tweets! "Hi everyone, we wanted you all to know directly from us, that Shannon & I have decided to end our relationship as boyfriend & girlfriend...," Derek tweeted that August. Finished Shannon, "However, we love and care about each other very much and will remain friends and in each others lives."

Derek is now married to his dance partner Hayley Erbert.

Though they dodged questions about their reported romance during season 18, a source told E! News that the eventual champs were just friends.

Showmance or Real Deal: This time, 'twas a showmance.

While they never technically dated, it didn't stop him from trying to woo his professional partner during season 10, even buying her gifts like a diamond necklace and a diamond ring, which she eventually gave back. "We had a fling," Cheryl later told Wendy Williams. "A little flirty fling. Like, a little flirt, flirt. That's it."

One of DWTS' most playful pairings, rumors continued about their relationship for all of season 10. And they weren't doing anything to stop them! Seriously, they staged an almost-kiss on a bed for one of their finale performances. Their banter continued eight cycles later when Erin signed on as the show's co-host.

Erin is now married to former NHL centre Jarret Stoll. They welcomed son Mack in July 2023.

Showmance or Real Deal: We're calling those Erin and Maks rumors a showmance.

While rumors ran rampant that the duo struck up a romance during season 17, the Pretty Little Liars star always denied that he was dating Peta.

#813. Even giant anteaters in remote Brazil have microplastics in their blood

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Gemma Conroy is a freelance journalist in Mexico City and editor of Nature Briefing: Careers.

Giant anteaters traipsing across Brazil's pristine wetlands and savannas have ingested traces of plastic pollutants. Credit: Sylvain Cordier/Gamma-Rapho via Getty

Some of Brazil’s wildlife have traces of plastic circulating in their blood — even if they live far from land used by humans, according to an analysis published on 11 November in Nature1.

Researchers measured the concentration of microplastics in the blood of 47 animals: 26 lowland tapirs (Tapirus terrestris) and 21 giant anteaters (Myrmecophaga tridactyla). The scientists found that, on average, the creatures carry similar levels of plastic to many humans — roughly 74 particles per millilitre of blood. The animals that lived closest to human infrastructure and waste-management facilities had the highest levels of microplastics in their blood.

But even those living more than 100 kilometres from a waste sites and 65 kilometres from human infrastructure showed traces of the pollutants. This indicates that plastics can reach wildlife living far from where the pollution originates, says study co-author Marcia de Almeida Monteiro Melo Ferraz, a conservation scientist at the University of British Columbia, Okanagan in Kelowna, Canada.

The findings are an important step to better understand how the particles impact wildlife, says Sofia Ya-Hsuan Liou, a geochemist at the National Taiwan University in Taipei.

Microplastics are tiny particles (smaller than five millimetres) with many different chemical compositions. They can travel through the environment in rainwater, rivers and the atmosphere. Although several studies have measured microplastics in wildlife, few have explored how the surrounding environment influences what animals ingest, says study co-author Michael Noonan, a quantitative ecologist at the University of British Columbia Okanagan.

To find out, Noonan, Ferraz and their colleagues collected and analysed blood samples from animals living across the Amazon rainforest, the Cerrado savanna and the huge and pristine Pantanal wetland between February 2021 and November 2022. The researchers also used GPS data to track the animals’ movements and their exposure to human footprint.

#812. A hidden star is plowing through Betelgeuse’s atmosphere, new evidence suggests

Something unusual is happening inside the enormous atmosphere of Betelgeuse, one of the most recognizable stars in the night sky. Astronomers have detected subtle changes in the star's shape that suggest something is moving through its outer layers, disturbing the surrounding gas like an unseen visitor making noise inside a house. (Metaphorically speaking.) New observations point to a likely culprit: Siwarha, a recently discovered companion star that appears to be traveling through Betelgeuse's atmosphere.

Betelgeuse is a massive red supergiant located in the constellation Orion, where it forms the famous hunter's shoulder. Although the star has fascinated astronomers for generations, it attracted worldwide attention in late 2019 and early 2020 when its brightness unexpectedly plunged to its lowest recorded level in more than 100 years. The event, known as the Great Dimming, raised questions about what was happening inside the aging star.

Now, observations from the U.S. National Science Foundation's Karl G. Jansky Very Large Array (NSF VLA) and the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) reveal that Betelgeuse's vast outer atmosphere has largely returned to normal. More intriguingly, the measurements provide new evidence that a nearby companion star is physically disturbing the giant star's atmosphere.

The research was led by Dr. Lynn D. Matthews, Principal Research Scientist and Assistant Director at MIT Haystack Observatory, working with scientists from the Center for Astrophysics | Harvard & Smithsonian, the University of Manchester, and the European Southern Observatory. The team analyzed observations gathered between 2021 and 2026 at seven radio frequencies ranging from 22 GHz to 485 GHz.

Different radio frequencies allow astronomers to examine different depths within a star's atmosphere. By combining the observations from both telescopes, the researchers reconstructed the structure of Betelgeuse's outer layers, beginning just above its visible surface and extending outward to several times its radius.

"It was the combination of the incredible data from the NSF VLA and ALMA that gave us a convincing result here," said Matthews. "The fact that we can use these facilities to actually resolve the disks of nearby stars is amazing."

Betelgeuse Recovers From Its Mysterious Great Dimming

The latest measurements also help scientists understand how Betelgeuse has changed since its extraordinary fading episode. Several months before the Great Dimming (when Betelgeuse ejected a billion tons of solar material, partially blocking our view), an earlier investigation led by Matthews detected unusually low temperatures in the star's atmosphere at radio wavelengths.

At the time, researchers suggested that turbulent convection deep inside Betelgeuse may have generated a shock wave that traveled outward and disrupted the surrounding gas. That disturbance could have helped trigger the enormous release of material that later formed dust and obscured part of the star's light.

The new observations indicate that the atmosphere has since warmed to temperatures more typical of Betelgeuse. At a distance of approximately 2.7 times the star's radius, the gas now has a measured brightness temperature of about 3,500 Kelvin (comparable to Betelgeuse's own surface temperature).

Astronomers Discover an Unexpectedly Cold Atmospheric Layer

The researchers also confirmed a feature that scientists had suspected existed for years: a region of unusually cool gas between Betelgeuse's visible surface and its higher atmospheric layer, known as the chromosphere.

Using ALMA at its highest observed frequencies, the team was able to probe closer to the star's surface than previous radio measurements had allowed. The results revealed temperatures falling to approximately 2,200 Kelvin, more than 1,000 degrees below the temperature of the visible surface, or photosphere.

This cool region corresponds to the "MOLsphere," a layer containing molecular gas that astronomers had previously identified primarily through infrared observations. The new radio measurements provide a much more direct examination of this elusive part of Betelgeuse's atmosphere and confirm the long-suspected "temperature minimum."

A Hidden Companion Star May Be Distorting Betelgeuse

One of the most intriguing discoveries involves Siwarha, the smaller star believed to orbit extremely close to Betelgeuse. Astronomers first proposed the companion's existence in 2024 as a possible explanation for a puzzling cycle in which Betelgeuse's brightness changes approximately every 2,100 days. Subsequent direct imaging and spectroscopic observations have provided additional support for the companion's existence.

The name Siwarha reflects its relationship with Betelgeuse. The giant star's name comes from the Arabic expression meaning "the hand of al-Jawza," while Siwarha means "her bracelet."

Unlike a planet or star traveling far from its host, Siwarha is believed to follow an orbit that takes it directly through Betelgeuse's extended atmosphere. Its estimated orbital distance is only about twice the red supergiant's radius.

"This companion is orbiting so close to the star that it actually passes through its extended atmosphere," Matthews explained.

As Siwarha moves along its orbit, it may push through the surrounding gas much like a fast boat cutting through water. The resulting wake could disturb the atmosphere, producing changes that astronomers can detect even though the smaller star itself remains invisible in the radio observations.

In fact, the researchers calculated that Siwarha is likely tens to hundreds of times too faint to be detected directly with the radio measurements they collected. Instead, they searched for indirect evidence of its presence by studying the shape of Betelgeuse's atmosphere.

Betelgeuse's Changing Shape Reveals New Clues

The scientists discovered that Betelgeuse does not always appear perfectly round at radio wavelengths. Its atmosphere sometimes develops a slightly stretched, oval appearance, and the timing of these changes appears to match the expected position of Siwarha.

To investigate this connection, the team measured the atmosphere's departure from a circular shape ("ellipticity") across observations taken at different times.

They found that Betelgeuse tends to look more elongated when Siwarha is expected to be at its greatest apparent separation from the giant star. When the companion is predicted to pass in front of or behind Betelgeuse from our perspective, the atmosphere appears rounder.

This relationship provides compelling evidence that the smaller star may be influencing the shape of Betelgeuse's outer layers through gravity and its physical passage through the gas.

The effect resembles noticing ripples spreading across a pond without being able to see what caused them. Although Siwarha remains too faint to identify directly at radio wavelengths, the changing shape of Betelgeuse's atmosphere may reveal its movement around the larger star.

Future Observations Could Reveal More About Betelgeuse

Despite the promising results, astronomers emphasize that additional observations are necessary to confirm the connection between Siwarha's orbit and the atmospheric distortions. Measurements covering more of the companion's orbital cycle, particularly at radio frequencies that have not yet been studied extensively, could help establish how strongly the smaller star affects Betelgeuse.

More advanced instruments may eventually provide an even clearer picture. The Next Generation Very Large Array, an observatory currently under development, is expected to make detailed studies of nearby stars and their atmospheres much easier.

Such observations could reveal not only how companion stars influence their massive neighbors, but also how aging red supergiants lose material as they approach the final stages of their lives. Understanding these interactions may help astronomers better explain the complicated processes that shape the evolution of enormous stars like Betelgeuse.

The findings were published in The Astronomical Journal in a paper titled "New Spatially Resolved Observations of Betelgeuse from the VLA and ALMA: Evidence for Atmospheric Perturbations from a Close Companion."

#811. NI can draw on strong club form in key window

Northern Ireland are top of Nations League Group B2 after four games

Despite being together for 16 straight days only a month ago, when Northern Ireland players reconvened this week for Nations League fixtures against Ukraine and Hungary there was still plenty of catching up to do.

Whether it be Pierce Charles' incredible double-save of Jarrod Bowen's penalty to preserve a point for Queens Park Rangers against West Ham, Isaac Price putting his own spot-kick woe behind him back at West Bromwich Albion, or Terry Devlin's double for Portsmouth against Swansea, there have been memorable moments aplenty for Michael O'Neill's squad back in club colours.

Most pleasing to the manager, however, will likely be the game time currently enjoyed by his players.

O'Neill has never shied away from the importance of a player's club situation to their international ambitions and, almost four years after his return to the Northern Ireland job, the message has clearly hit home.

Of what is a 24-man squad for games against Ukraine on Saturday and Hungary three days later, nine players made either a permanent or loan switch during the summer.

And while once the former Stoke City boss had to heavily rely on players who were getting precious few minutes in between international windows, now the group is full of regulars across England top three divisions.

Excluding the uncapped trio of Dermot Mee, Eoin Kenny and Braiden Graham, the remainder of the panel for this double-header have averaged over 1,000 minutes of club action during the 2026-27 campaign.

Of that group, only Tom Atcheson, who has been carrying a knock, Paddy McNair, Kieran Morrison and Callum Marshall have started fewer than four games since the side's most recent international against Georgia last month.

Watch on BBC iPlayer and BBC Two NI from19:15 GMT; Listen on BBC Sounds and BBC Radio Ulster; Watch, listen, live text and clips on BBC Sport app & website

The next step, O'Neill feels, is to have more and more joining the likes of Conor Bradley, Daniel Ballard, Trai Hume and Shea Charles in the Premier League.

"There's a lot of players who are playing on a regular basis at their clubs, which is a real positive," said O'Neill, who is without Ballard, Bradley and Arsenal's Ceadach O'Neill for this window through injuries.

"I think at this stage of their career they should be looking up. Our players that play in the Championship hopefully will have aspirations to play in the Premier League, and I think we have players that are capable of that.

"A lot of these players are still around that 20, 21, 22 age group but they're capable of taking that step.

"The more players we can get to the Premier League will help us as a nation, there's no doubt about that. I'm pleased where a lot of the players are at this minute in time but I still think individually with their clubs they've got a lot of scope to grow and develop as well."

Birthdays and broken lamps - at home with the Charles brothers

Kenny's background 'not that important' to O'Neill

Two of those playing at League One level this season are attackers Jamie Donley and Marshall, both at Luton Town under Jack Wilshere.

While a regular goalscorer remains elusive for O'Neill - the side have scored just once in their past four home games and that was a Donley penalty against Luxembourg - both have found the net at Kenilworth Road in recent weeks.

Donley, who is on loan from Tottenham Hotspur, plays in a deeper role at the club than the false nine position he occupies for Northern Ireland and has scored three times with two assists since a goalless four-game Nations League window across the end of September and start of October.

"I think Jamie has played well for us as a nine. He's different in terms of what you might look for in a profile as a nine. He comes and links the play and plays a little bit deeper," said O'Neill.

"I don't think you can compare, with all due respect, the chances that he may get playing for Luton in League One where they're a strong team, to playing for Northern Ireland at Nations League B. They're not overly comparable. It's not down to position for Jamie. It's what he brings to the team.

"The most important thing for me is that Jamie comes in confident to our camps. The fact that he's scoring goals at his club can only help him, regardless of what position we play him in."

Marshall is one of the few in the squad still struggling for starts at club level, although he has found the net four times in League One since joining the Hatters from West Ham in the summer.

The 21-year-old, who had previous loan spells at West Brom, Huddersfield Town and Vfl Bochum, has featured just once in Northern Ireland's past five games and is yet to score at international level.

"I encouraged him to make the move [to Luton] on a permanent basis because I think that you go through a loan scenario and it's difficult," said O'Neill.

"I've been on the other side of that as a manager and brought players in on loan so I know that sometimes it's not always in the best interest of the player.

"Callum going to Luton, I think, was positive with the fact that Jack Wilshere really wanted him and they obviously had to pay a decent fee for him.

"It's now down to Callum really. He's at a club that I think should suit him as a striker. Callum is capable of scoring goals and the ball's in his court now."

#810. Prince George’s Secret Talent Proves He’s Spreading His Wings

Prince George put his artistic talents on display in the latest issue of Country Life magazine, which features a drawing of a kingfisher done by the 13-year-old.

Prince George is displaying a crowning achievement.

The eldest son of Prince William and Kate Middleton showed off his immense artist talent in an upcoming issue of Country Life magazine, guest-edited by his father, with a drawing of a kingfisher done by the 13-year-old.

George’s drawing features the bird with dark green and yellow plumage—and the signature pointed bill of a kingfisher—perched on top of a piece of wood, gazing off into the distance.

And he’s had a knack for the arts for years. Back in 2022, he drew a portrait of a reindeer that his family—including siblings Princess Charlotte, 11, and Prince Louis, 8—shared as their Christmas card on Instagram that year.

It's no wonder that he has picked up a palette, as both his mother and his grandfather King Charles III are quite artistically inclined as well. Kate received her degree in art history and has previously displayed her skills, posting a sketch of St. Andrews in Scotland in 2021 as well as photographing the royal family over the years. Charles, meanwhile, is known for his landscapes, often depicting Balmoral Castle in Scotland, Windsor Castle and other royal properties.

As for Kate, she shared a look at the whole family’s art skills in 2025, posting portraits she and her children had drawn to Instagram that had provided “a moment of connection”—although she did not say who had drawn which portrait.

In recent months George has been keeping busy not only with art but also as a student at Eton College while he prepares to one day take the throne following his grandfather and father.

"There’s lots of things to think about with that," William noted on an October episode of The Reluctant Traveler With Eugene Levy. "But obviously, I want to create a world in which my son is proud of what we do and a world and a job that actually does impact people’s lives for the better.”

And much of that desire comes from what he and brother Prince Harry experienced during their childhoods, adding, "That is caveated with I hope we don’t go back to some of the practices in the past that Harry and I had to grow up in. And I’ll do everything I can to make sure we don’t regress in that situation."

The Wales family's team of five consisting of Prince William, Kate Middleton, Prince George, Princess Charlotte and Prince Louis attended the August 2026 Commonwealth Games in Glasgow.

Per tradition, William, Kate and their kids joined royal family members in closing out the June 2026 Trooping the Colour ceremonial parade with a wave from the balcony of London's Buckingham Palace.

The Wales family hopped over to St. George's Chapel at Windsor Castle to celebrate Easter in April 2026.

The couple and their two eldest children served up another sweet family moment at Wimbledon in July 2025.

Louis was captivated by the flypast he watched with his mom, dad and siblings from Buckingham Palace's balcony that took place on the 80th anniversary of VE Day in May 2025.

Louis, George and Charlotte rode off to London's Westminster Abbey for their grandfather King Charles III's coronation ceremony in May 2023—though the monarch immediately acceded to the throne following the death of his mother Queen Elizabeth II in September 2022.

As part of the coronation activities, William and Kate reminded their kids of the importance of service by bringing all three of them to volunteer at the Big Help Out in May 2023.

Kicking off another year, William and Kate walked George, Charlotte and Louis to their "settling in" day at their primary school in the Berkshire countryside in September 2022.

Charlotte gave her dad a thumbs-up as they attended the Commonwealth Games' swimming event with Kate in August 2022.

While celebrating the Platinum Jubilee of Queen Elizabeth II in June 2022, Louis sweetly wrapped his arm around his mom.

He also joined his older siblings in a carriage ride to mark the momentous occasion.

As William, Kate, George and Charlotte headed to 2022's Easter service at St. George's Chapel in Windsor, fans might have noticed some bunny was missing. However, the service may have been too long for Louis, who was only 4 years old at the time and already proving he could get into some adorable mischief.

Making his Trooping the Colour balcony debut nearly two months after his first birthday, Louis gave a little wave alongside his parents and siblings at the June 2019 event.

Joined by Prince Harry and Meghan Markle, King Charles III and Queen Camilla and the Middletons, William held the hands of then-3-year-old Charlotte and almost 5-year-old George as they walked into Chapel Royal at St James's Palace for the July 2018 christening of Louis.

#809. Bristol City give Skubala opportunity to improve form

Michael Skubala has won five of his 15 league games in charge of Bristol City

Bristol City will give under-pressure head coach Michael Skubala the chance to improve their results, particularly at home, says chief executive Charlie Boss.

The Robins have lost their past four Championship matches at Ashton Gate, culminating in last Saturday's 5-0 drubbing by Norwich City which left them in 17th place.

"The game against Norwich was a long way short of our standards and in the days that followed there have been a lot of tough and honest conversations around the building," said Boss in a video message on the club website., external

"Earlier this week the board met and we agreed to give Michael Skubala the opportunity to turn around the home form."

Skubala led Lincoln City to the League One title last season before joining Bristol City on a three-year-deal in May.

However, a run of only two wins from their past 10 matches has led to supporters voicing their concerns.

"A lot of fans made their feelings known loud and clear at Ashton Gate on Saturday and I want them to know everybody shares their frustration from the owners, the board and the players," added Boss.

"Michael Skubala more than anyone knows we need to improve - we wouldn't have made this decision if we didn't believe that together we can get through this difficult period."

Bristol City's next Championship match is at second-placed Middlesbrough on Saturday, 21 November (15:00 GMT) before home games against Wrexham and Swansea sandwich a trip to West Bromwich Albion.

Dancing With the Stars' Daniella Karagach exclusively revealed to E! News what it was like competing against husband Pasha Pashkov during the dance battle on the Nov. 10 Grammy Night episode.

Daniella Karagach always finds her rhythm with husband Pasha Pashkov.

While the Dancing With the Stars pros were up against each other during the dance battle on the Nov. 10 Grammy Night episode, it didn’t feel like they were in competition as they danced the rumba alongside partners Ezra Frech and Amber Glenn to Brandy and Monica’s “The Boy Is Mine.”

“I wouldn't think of it as against them,” Karagach exclusively shared with E! News. “We were literally just practicing our rumba as if we were the only ones on the floor, and then we get to share the stage at the end of the day with them.”

And the 33-year-old hit just the right step with her husband of 12 years, adding, “When we got to block this for the first time with them, it was just so fun.”

Her partner Frech, 21, also had a ball dancing with Glenn, 27, and Pashkov, 40, telling E! it felt more like a team dance than a dance battle.

“Amber and I didn't get to be on the same team—the team dance,” he recalled of the Nov. 2 episode. “Now we did. We got it tonight.”

Throughout the competition, Karagach and Pashkov—who share 3-year-old daughter Nikita—have shared what it’s like for them in the ballroom, with Karagach noting it never feels like they’re competing.

“Literally he's my teammate,” she told E! News after the DWTS premiere. “He's my partner. He's my rock.”

“It’s just never a competition,” she added. “He's either helping me or I'm helping him.”

And that closeness has extended to Frech and Glenn as Karagach said the quartet “have dinner all together.”

“We go to our house and just unwind,” she continued. “It's just the best time. It doesn't feel like a competition.”

And Frech could not agree more, adding, “Pasha and Amber are—they're unbelievable. I love them so much.”

#807. NASA smashed into an asteroid. Now Hera is closing in to see what happened

The European Space Agency's Hera spacecraft has reached an important milestone in its mission to investigate a historic asteroid collision. For the first time, its onboard camera has captured the two asteroids Didymos and Dimorphos as separate objects rather than a single point of light.

The asteroid pair is currently about 197 million kilometers from Earth. Hera obtained the new image on the evening of October 18 using its black-and-white Asteroid Framing Camera, while the spacecraft was approximately 1,280 kilometers from its targets.

"With this image, the smaller Dimorphos asteroid becomes visible for the first time," explains Michael Kueppers. "Before this acquisition, the spacecraft was still resolving the Didymos system as a single dot. But now, even though Dimorphos is made up of only around one pixel in this initial image, it is clearly well separated from its parent body."

The breakthrough image follows a successful series of maneuvers designed to slow Hera as it approaches the asteroid system. Earlier in October, the spacecraft fired its thrusters twice, with one week between the maneuvers. These adjustments reduced its speed relative to the asteroids to just 20 meters per second, allowing mission controllers to carefully manage the remaining approach.

Although the two asteroids appear tiny in the initial image, they are substantial objects. Dimorphos measures about 151 meters across, making it roughly comparable in size to the Great Pyramid of Giza. Its larger companion, Didymos, is approximately 780 meters in diameter, slightly smaller than the height of Dubai's Burj Khalifa, the world's tallest building.

Dimorphos travels around Didymos at an average separation of just 1.15 kilometers, moving at a speed of approximately 18 centimeters per second.

"For the very first time we are seeing through Hera's own eyes the very double asteroid system that the mission was designed and built for," adds mission manager Ian Carnelli.

"Our views will grow much sharper as Hera comes closer. We will unveil the first detailed images of Dimorphos -- the first object in the Solar System to have had its orbit measurably shifted by human action -- on 25 November."

Uncovering the Aftermath of NASA's Historic Asteroid Collision

Hera's arrival will give scientists an opportunity to examine the results of a groundbreaking planetary defense experiment conducted four years earlier.

On September 26, 2022, NASA's Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) spacecraft deliberately collided with Dimorphos at approximately 6.1 kilometers per second. The impact blasted debris as far as 10,000 kilometers into space and shortened the asteroid's orbital period around Didymos by roughly 33 minutes.

The experiment demonstrated that a spacecraft could deliberately change an asteroid's motion, an achievement with potentially enormous implications for protecting Earth from future asteroid threats.

However, the collision also produced results that scientists are still trying to fully explain. The asteroid's orbital change was substantially greater than computer simulations had predicted, raising questions about its physical properties and how it responded to the impact.

Researchers still do not know whether DART left a crater on Dimorphos or significantly altered the asteroid's overall shape. They also need more precise measurements of its composition, internal structure, and mass to understand why the collision was so effective.

Answering these questions is essential for transforming the 'kinetic impact' approach into a reliable planetary defense strategy.

Hera Prepares for a Detailed Asteroid Investigation

Over the coming months, Hera will carry out a detailed 'crash site investigation' to uncover what NASA's collision actually did to Dimorphos.

The spacecraft will use a collection of scientific instruments to examine the asteroid and its surroundings. It will also release two small satellites, known as 'CubeSats', each approximately the size of a shoebox, to gather additional observations from much closer distances. The investigation is expected to eventually include landing operations.

Together, these measurements should help scientists better understand how asteroids respond to high-speed impacts and improve predictions of how future deflection attempts might work.

Anyone interested in following Hera's journey can explore the mission through the Hera Space Companion. More than a conventional AI chatbot, this interactive communication platform is connected to the mission and designed to make the European Space Agency's first planetary defense mission accessible to the public.

Materials provided by European Space Agency (ESA). Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

The ice giants' skewed magnetic fields are a window into the high-pressure, high-temperature environment deep inside Uranus and Neptune.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The posided magnetic fields of Uranus and Neptune may stem from extreme conditions lying within their deep interior. Unravelling the mystery behind the magnetic fields of these worlds is giving us new insight into the little-known interiors of the ice giants.

Only one spacecraft has ever visited Uranus and Neptune, the Voyager 2 spacecraft which spend past Uranus in January 1986 and Neptune in August 1989. Voyager 2 found that their planetary magnetic fields were, to put it bluntly, wonky. Uranus’ magnetic field was offset from its rotational axis by 59 degrees and isn’t even centered on the planet’s core, but instead is only two-thirds of the way down. Neptune is similar, with a disordered magnetic field offset by 47 degrees and centered halfway between the core and its visible cloud tops.If we compare these planets to Earth, which has a stable magnetic field tilted by just 11 degrees to our planet’s rotation, we can see how extreme the magnetic fields of the ice giants are.

Various explanations for the strange magnetic fields of the ice giants have been put forward over the years. Uranus as a whole is tilted by 97 degrees and effectively rolls around the sun, and speculation is that billions of years ago it was knocked on its side by a collision with a long-lost Earth-sized planet. Could this collision have also skewed its magnetic field?

This might be a plausible explanation were Neptune’s magnetic field also not similarly skewed without having experienced a collision. Clearly, whatever the cause, it must be intrinsic to the nature of the two ice giant planets. Now, a new study by scientists in the U.S. and the UK, based on computer simulations and Voyager 2’s measurements of the two planets’ magnetic fields, may have found a solution.

The solution to the weird magnetic fields of the solar system's ice giants may come down to how planets generate their magnetic field through the dynamo effect. This arises from the swirling, convective motion of an electrically conducting liquid within a rotating body, which is able to generate and maintain a powerful magnetic field.

Inside Earth, the electrically conducting fluid is the molten iron in the outer part of our planet’s core, and the magnetic field that it generates has clear north and south poles – what we call a dipole, a phenomenon that we can also see in the two magnetic poles of a simple bar magnet.

However, the conditions inside Uranus and Neptune are somewhat different. As ice giants, they contain a lot of volatiles – ammonia, hydrogen, helium, methane, and water surrounding a probable rocky core. Furthermore, Uranus and Neptune are substantially larger than Earth, with 14.5 and 17 times the mass of our planet, respectively. This increased mass creates crushing conditions within the interior of the ice giants.

"Deep inside Uranus and Neptune, pressures and temperatures become extremely high," research team leader Chi Yan of the University of Texas at Austin, who led the new findings, said in a statement. "Under those conditions, which can cause water molecules to break apart into ions, the material may become increasingly electrically conductive with depth."

Given the increasing electrical conductivity and the compositions of the two planets, the computer simulations were able to replicate the bizarre magnetic fields of Uranus and Neptune. This showed how the magnetic-field structure co-evolves alongside changes in the fluid motion driven by convection and the temperature inside the planets.

It also seems that this co-evolution might not yet be over. The simulations indicate that the magnetic fields of both planets can change quite significantly in the space of just a few decades.

"Earth’s magnetic tilt drifts by only a degree or so over 50 years," said Yan. "Our models show the ice giants can behave very differently. In some stretches, the tilt swings by tens of degrees within decades. In others, it shifts only slightly over the same span."

NASA have prioritized a new mission to return to Uranus in the early 2040s, while the China National Space Administration’s Tianwen-4 mission launching to Jupiter in 2029 will deploy a small probe to carry onwards to Uranus via a gravitational slingshot. Until then, scientists are coming up with creative ways to not have to rely only on the 40-year-old Voyager 2 measurements of the magnetic fields.

For example, Tom Stallard of Northumbria University in the UK, who is a co-author with Yan on the new research paper, has been leading James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) observations of the faint infrared auroral lights on both Uranus and Neptune. Aurorae are generated when charged particles on the solar wind interact with a planet’s magnetic field, driving some of those charged particles into the atmosphere above the magnetic poles. (Neptune actually has a quadrupolar component, muddling its defined north and south magnetic poles.) As such, the location of aurorae is a good indicator of what’s going on with a planet’s magnetic field.

"We are busy working on what’s contained within these observations, but the shape and structure of the aurora, as well as other weird patterns in the ionosphere [upper atmosphere], promise to provide us with a way of understanding how the magnetic fields have changed, [which is] an important stepping stone," said Stallard.

The hope is that by combining JWST’s observations of the aurora with Voyager 2’s magnetic-field measurements and the results of the computer simulations, it will be possible to estimate the configuration of the magnetic fields on Uranus and Neptune today and see how they compare to the 1980s.

This would provide an experimental test to help show whether the new model describing the magnetic fields is on the right track, although we won’t know for sure until a new mission arrives in the ice giants’ backyard.

The findings were described on 3 November in the journal Communications Physics.

Keith Cooper is a freelance science journalist and editor in the United Kingdom, and has a degree in physics and astrophysics from the University of Manchester. He's the author of "The Contact Paradox: Challenging Our Assumptions in the Search for Extraterrestrial Intelligence" (Bloomsbury Sigma, 2020) and has written articles on astronomy, space, physics and astrobiology for a multitude of magazines and websites.

#805. Dua Lipa, SZA and Tame Impala Set to Headline Coachella 2027

Ahead of Coachella 2027, Dua Lipa, SZA and Tame Impala have been confirmed as headliners for the annual two-weekend music festival in Southern California.

You should know that Coachella 2027 is already shaping up to be the best yet.

After all, Dua Lipa, Tame Impala and SZA are officially headlining the iconic California desert the upcoming music festival, set to take place the second and third weekends of April 2027.

Dua will own Friday at the festival, where the "Levitating" artist will be joined by the likes of Madonna, Zara Larsson, Steve Lacy and Jisoo.

Tame Impala will command the stage on Saturday—the lineup also including artists such as Phoebe Bridgers, Weezer and Robyn—while SZA is the top billing on Sunday, with Kygo, Becky G and Don Toliver among the other performers.

For her part, Dua will take the stage for her first solo set at the annual festival, exactly 10 years after making a guest appearance in 2017 during Martin Garrix’s set.

And while training season for the headliner stage has just started, the forthcoming performance may mark the first new musical release since her 2024 album Radical Optimism. (Not to mention, Dua’s frequent appearances outside of Electric Lady Studios in New York the last few months have gotten fans levitating.)

Following her wedding to Callum Turner in May, the “Training Season” singer hinted at what was to come for her fourth studio album—noting her source of inspiration has shifted.

"Talking about being heartbroken is a very common thing,” the 31-year-old told Vogue Italia in an August interview. “When I was younger, I found much more inspiration in the search and desire. And that’s because feeling broken is a very strong and loud emotion.”

As she has hit the studio again, Dua has set out some new rules for herself.

“I want to discover what happens when you truly find love,” she explained. “I’m interested in the complexities of a relationship, its quieter aspects, the little thing.”

SZA, meanwhile, is no stranger to the Coachella stage, making her Coachella debut in 2018 and even making an appearance last year with Justin Bieber to perform their hit duet “Snooze.”

But while the performance during weekend two of the festival was special for fans, the 36-year-old shut down rumors she was tapped by the festival to act as Justin’s understudy if he failed to make a performance.

“Lmao who made this up?” SZA wrote on Instagram last year. “I’ve seen this 4 times now. I’m in New York no one paid me a dime. Wishing everyone the best.”

During her upcoming Coachella performance, though, SZA might just kill fans with some new tracks. After all, she confirmed in a recent Instagram comment she would “indeed” be returning with new music after releasing SOS Deluxe: Lana last year.

And as for Tame Impala? The musician (real name: Kevin Parker) last hit the Coachella stage in 2019. And considering he’s put out The Slow Rush and Deadbeats in the interim, fans will want to be right there where he’s performing next year—especially if Jennie makes an appearance to run from sunlight, Dracula.

#804. Referee observer banned for discriminatory comments

Brian Curson has been involved in football for more than 40 years

A Pro Ref referee observer has been suspended for nine weeks and fined Â£200 for making discriminatory remarks after a match he was working at.

Brian Curson had visited Kenilworth Road to assess the officials at the League One fixture between Luton Town and Rotherham United on 15 November 2025.

An allegation was made that Curson made two discriminatory comments in the lounge at Luton's stadium after the game, which led to the Football Association investigation.

Curson was charged with acting in an improper manner and/or using abusive and/or insulting words.

It was considered an 'aggravated breach', using words which included a reference - whether express or implied - to ethnic origin, race or nationality.

Curson, who no longer works for Pro Ref, said that he did not recall making the comments but the FA commission "was satisfied on the balance of probabilities" that they had been made.

The FA requested a time-based sanction because of Curson's role in the sport, as a player would serve a suspension of between nine and 12 matches.

It was determined that, taking into account Curson's experience and role on the day of the match, he should be suspended for nine weeks.

Curson was also told he must attend a mandatory education programme, and received a warning as to future conduct.

Dancing With the Stars pro Jenna Johnson confirmed to E! News that a “little accident” such as a broken nose can’t stop her and Harry Shum Jr. as they look ahead to the semifinals.

Jenna Johnson is putting her best nose, er, foot forward.

Despite taking an accidental hit to the face the day before the Dancing With the Stars quarterfinals on Nov. 10, Johnson confirmed she isn’t going to let the broken bone affect her and Harry Shum Jr.’s performances.

“It's so funny, these little accidents always happen,” she exclusively told E! News following the show’s Grammys night. “Dance is a physical contact sport, and I want to always represent dancers as athletes. Just like any other professional athlete would get a little dinged up here or there, they would still go compete.”

“They kept asking me,” she added, like, ‘Do you want someone to dance for you?’ And I was like, ‘No, I love this dance. I've loved dancing this week with Harry. Like, no one is keeping me off the freaking dance floor.’”

And a good thing, too, since their salsa to “Die With a Smile” earned an impressive 29 out of a possible 30 points.

Plus, it helped that the people in Johnson’s life all have a nose for how to best carry her through the performance, despite the injury.

“I've been so supported,” the 32-year-old said. “So, I have to thank all the teams that were there for me last night. But yeah, it's just part of the show.”

Shum, however, wasn’t ready for his partner to brush off her accomplishment.

“It also speaks to you,” the Grey’s Anatomy star emphasized. “Dancers don't get enough credit for how much pain they go through—their feet, injuries in their knees, their back, and like your nose.”

He added, “And to say like, ‘Nope, I'm going to keep going,’ because you love to perform. But also, you work so hard for something and you said, ‘No, I'm not going to let this stop me if it doesn't need to.’”

And stop her it won’t, with the two ready to lead each other on a merry dance all the way through the semifinals.

“Jenna always has a strategy,” Shum emphasized, “and I follow whatever she has in store.”

Meanwhile, Johnson noted it truly takes two to tango.

“You are so smart when it comes to things,” she added. “I love that leading up to this moment, I think we were very thoughtful about what we wanted to do in the semifinals if we had the opportunity to be here. And I'm super excited.”
